heading: 1.3.1 ASA Node
text:
1.3.1 ASA Node
An ASA node is a stack of a single Physical Layer, a single Data Link Layer and one or more Application
Stream Encapsulators/Decapsulators. In the case of optional Link Aggregation, the single Physical
Layer is replaced by the Link Aggregation Sublayer and a multitude of Physical Layers.

heading: 1.3.2 ASA Device
text:
1.3.2 ASA Device
An ASA device is the smallest unit or module that contains one or more compliant ASA nodes
belonging to the same ASA SerDes Branch.

heading: 1.3.3 ASA Link
text:
1.3.3 ASA Link
An ASA Link is a pair of ASA devices connected together on their MDIs with a cable.

heading: 1.3.4 ASA Motion Link
text:
1.3.4 ASA Motion Link
ASA Motion Link is the brand name for all ASA technologies/devices. Devices based on chapters 2-7
of the ASA Transceiver Specification arereferred to as “ASA Motion Link” or “ASA Motion Link
SerDes”. Device based on chapter 8 are referred to as “ASA Motion Link Ethernet” (MLE).

heading: 1.3.5 ASA SerDes Branch
text:
1.3.5 ASA SerDes Branch
An ASA SerDes Branch is a multitude of ASA devices connected in a tree (non-loop) topology and
made up of one or more point to point connections between ASA nodes of separate ASA devices.

heading: 1.3.6 Root Node/Device
text:
1.3.6 Root Node/Device
The Root node/device is the device containing the ASA node, which is in control by running OAM
sessions with all other ASA nodes in the SerDes Branch. There is only a single root node in each
SerDes Branch (designated by nodeID=1).

heading: 1.3.7 Leaf Node/Device
text:
1.3.7 Leaf Node/Device
The Leaf node/device is a device in the SerDes Branch containing a single ASA node, which is not the
Root node/device.

heading: 1.3.8 Branch Device
text:
1.3.8 Branch Device
The Branch device is a device in the SerDes Branch containing two or more ASA nodes, which is not
the Root node/device.

heading: 1.3.9 Downstream (Dn)
text:
1.3.9 Downstream (Dn)
Downstream direction with Downstream transmitter and Downstream receiver make up the high
bandwidth part of the ASA asymmetric half-duplex communication. It is abbreviated as Dn.
1.3.10Upstream (Up)
Upstream direction with Upstream transmitter and Upstream receiver make up the low bandwidth
part of the ASA asymmetric half-duplex communication. It is abbreviated as Up.
1.3.11Data Link Layer Container
One fixed size unit (per direction Downstream and Upstream) of the time division multiplex scheme
in a point-to-point ASA link.
1.3.12Near-side
A node is near-side to the root node, when OAM containers from the root node are directly coming
through the PLP_RX of that same node.
1.3.13Far-side
A node is far-side to the root node, when OAM containers from the root node have to pass another
node in the same device first to get to the same node.
1.3.14Clock Leader
In ASA the Clock Leader is located in the root node. It is the one node, which is not adjusting its PTB
clock to another node in the SerDes branch, but is providing the reference clock for the SerDes
branch.
1.3.15Local Clock Leader
The Local Clock Leader is the Far-side node on a Branch-Device, which is providing the PTB reference
clock towards the Leaf Nodes. There is a local clock leader for each point-to-point link. In a Branch
Device, each Far-side Node is a Local Clock Leader.
1.3.16Clock Follower
The clock follower is the Near-side node on a Branch-Device or Leaf Node, which is following the PTB
reference clock. Any non-root node device can have only one single Clock Follower on a particular
ASA Branch Device. There is a single follower at the Near-side of each P2P link.

Features Overview
ASA specifies a half-duplex Physical Layer on Automotive STP and coax cables for asymmetric payload
data rates split between Downstream (high rate) and Upstream (low rate) direction and separated by
an Inter Burst Gap (IBG). The Physical Layer supports 5 fixed-rate Speed Grades in Downstream and 2
fixed-rate Speed Grades in Upstream direction. For all Speed Grade combinations, each direction is
given transmit access to the cable for a defined fraction of a constant time-division duplexing (TDD)
cycle.
A Startup procedure supports automatic startup of link partners into Normal Mode as well as startup
into Test Mode via cable interface. See section 4.

heading: 2.4 ASA Transceiver State Diagram

figures.title: Overview of ASA half-duplexing Physical Layer and time-division Data Link Layer access
Overall ASA Transceiver state diagram

text:
The Startup also supports node enumeration and enables configurability of the entire SerDes branch
from the root node.
The optional feature of Light Sleep enables a duty cycling of the Physical Layer between active and
disabled state in the time scale of typical sensor and display event periods.
The Data Link Layer supports multiplexing and demultiplexing of application and internal data
streams onto and from the Physical Layer. The multiplexing of fixed size containers is controlled by a
programmable, deterministic, cyclic time-division access mechanism dubbed a Mapper. The
demultiplexer supports forwarding of streams in a SerDes Branch tree topology as well as stream
duplication (multicast up to 4 nodes). Data Link Layer behavior is configured through ASA registers
(see section 3) accessed by the ASA internal communication protocol OAM (Operations,
Administration, Maintenance). See section 5.
ASA specifies a mandatory logical clock throughout the SerDes Branch called PTB (Precision Time
Base).
The Data Link Layer optionally supports link-based security with authentication and encryption (see
6).
ASA specifies ASA-internal exchange formats of common application data types or interfaces for the
payload of Data Link Layer containers. See section 7.
An ASA device implements a subset of the ASEP types relevant to the application, where each ASEP
type may be present with one or more instances.

Power On state is entered at the time, when a stable power supply to the device containing the ASA
node is established (such that volatile memory is persistent). The duration from entering the Power-
On state to entering Normal Mode state shall be 100ms or less. Of these 100ms, a maximum of up to
30ms can be spent in Power-On state.
The state diagrams for Startup and startup-triggered Test Mode are described in 4.3.3.1. OAM config
is described in 5.9. The state diagrams of Light Sleep are described in 5.8.3.
Fail State is entered when Link Loss spans 3 consecutive TDD bursts or more (see also 3.2.13).

heading: 3 ASA Registers

tables.title: ASA register address fields

text:
ASA Registers
Each ASA node has its own ASA register map. An ASA Device with more than one node carries a
complete ASA register map for each node. The register map is divided into domains, see Table 3-2.
The number of register subdomains 4 and 5 depends on the number of implemented ASE and ASD.
Register domains and registers for optional features are part of this optional feature and only exist,
when this optional feature is present.
Access: A register can be accessible only locally or through OAM. Access through OAM implies local
access. When a register is accessible through OAM, it can be accessed by the root node under any
condition or it can be accessed only with an authenticated message (enforced by the optional feature
Security Entity, see section 6).
Privilege:A register, which requires the access privilege “authenticated by security” can only be
accessed locally, if security is not present. (INFORMATIVE: access restrictions refer to limitations that
have to be enforced for interoperability; it does not impact accessibility in non-ASA operation
modes).
ASA register addresses are given in the formatof four fields “d.a.(m:l)”or five fields “d.i.a.(m:l)”
depending on the domain/layer, where the fields are described in Table 3-1.
Address
Definition/Description | Range of values
Field

6-8 … reserved

(only used, when domain is 4 or 5) | 1-63 … DLP ID

Table 3-1: ASA register address fields
All ASA registers per address“d.a.”or“d.i.a.”are 16 bitswide. The addition of “m:l” is used for
indexing with these 16 bits (“d.a.m:l”or“d.i.a.m:l”).
If “l” is omitted(“d.a.m”or“d.i.a.m”), only a single bit is addressed/described.
If “l” and “m” are omitted(“d.a”or“d.i.a”), the whole register is addressed/described.
All address fields are given as integer numbers in this section 3 and the rest of the specification. The
register number “a” is given as a 4-digit integer number.

The default reset value of each register is 0, unless otherwise stated in the register definition.
Register Types and Access
ASA Registers have one of three read/write types: read/write (R/W), read-only (RO) and read-only
with automatic reset, when they are read (self-clearing = SC).
ASA Register access is either L=local only or by O=OAM (which implies local access).
ASA Register privilege through OAM access is either by root node only (RID=rootID) or only, when
access is from root node and the link is protected by security (A=authenticated).
User Registers
Register addresses with d=0 are accessible by OAM channel. Number of registers and register
contents are left to the implementer.

ASEP Registers
ASEP Registers use a subdomain identifier “i" after the domain toidentify the ASE or ASD (see also
section 3).
Registers in the address range 4/5.i.0001-0099 are defined for all ASEPs.
Registers in the address range 4/5.i.0051-0099 are for each address the same register for all
subdomains.
Registers in the address range 4.i.0100-0199 are defined for all ASE (regardless of protocol or serve a
generic function).
Registers in the address range 5.i.0100-0199 are defined for all ASD (regardless of protocol or serve a
generic function).
Registers starting from address 4/5.i.0200 and higher are specific to each ASEP and semantics change
based on streamType (see section 3.5.1.2).

text:
3.5.1.1 Full Packet ID (4/5.i.0001, 4/5.i.0002, 4/5.i.0003)
Each fullPacketID[47:0] is associated with each DLP_TX_ID and each DLP_RX_ID port and therefore in
the ASEP address space, but managed by the DLL.
It is incremented for each container sent for this DLP_TX, whereas the lower 5 bits fullPacketID[4:0]
are copied into the container header. See 5.2.2.4.
At the receiver side (sinking DLP_RX), the fullPacketID[47:0] is incremented for every correctly
received container. See 5.3.2.1.
The register fullPacketID resets to 0.
For the special case of the FoFa, where ASEP Stream Type is“Return OAM”or“ForwardData”, the
register has no function. See 5.4.

heading: 4.2.1 PCS Reset Function
text:
4.2.1 PCS Reset Function
The PCS reset function initializes all PCS functions including all LFSR and the registers described in
section 3.2. The PCS reset is executed at Power-On state.
The PCS reset is also executed at Fail state unless otherwise defined for a particular register or
function.
Soft Reset through register (see section 3.2.7) is a subset of PCS reset as Soft Reset does not impact
configuration values.

heading: 4.2.2.2.1 Synchronization to PTB
text:
4.2.2.2.1 Synchronization to PTB
In an ASA SerDes Branch topology beyond point-to-point, it is important to keep TDD cycles aligned
after the StartTDD command (see 5.5.3.9). The PCS in the root node (i.e. clock leader) or node, which
is link-local clock leader, therefore starts a new TDD cycle every 6844 PTB tics (with a tolerance of
±1).

4.2.2.5.1 Downstream Speed Grade 1, 2 and 3
The physical layer block tx_phy_block<5183:0> (SG 1 and 2) or tx_phy_block<5759:0> (SG 3) is

scrambler is advanced by one shift for every one bit in tx_phy_block and the first output bit of the

heading: 4.2.2.6 PAM2 Mapping
text:
4.2.2.6 PAM2 Mapping
The PCS transmit function shall map consecutive bits of tx_phy_block_scr to consecutive PAM2
symbols starting with the MSB of tx_phy_block_scr.
Each bit of tx_phy_block_scr is mapped to one PAM2 symbol M(j) as follows:
0 maps to 1,
1 maps to -1.

heading: 4.2.2.7 PAM4 Gray Encoding
text:
4.2.2.7 PAM4 Gray Encoding
The PCS transmit function shall map consecutive pairs of bits of tx_phy_block_scr to consecutive
Gray-coded PAM4 symbols starting with the MSB of tx_phy_block_scr.
Each pair of bits, {MSB, LSB} of tx_phy_block_scr is mapped to one Gray-coded PAM4 symbol M(j) as
follows:
{0, 0} maps to 1,
{0, 1} maps to 1/3,
{1, 1} maps to -1/3,
{1, 0} maps to -1.

heading: 4.2.3.1 Burst synchronization
text:
4.2.3.1 Burst synchronization
Using the symbols provided by the PMA Receive, the PCS shall detect and decode the
Resynchronization Header (see 4.2.2.3) and use it to detect and correct signal polarity as well as align
to the physical layer blocks.

heading: 4.2.3.2 PCS descrambler
text:
4.2.3.2 PCS descrambler
The PCS shall use the synchronization of 4.2.3.1 to start/stop the side stream scrambler to and
reverse the transmit side scrambling by applying the same operation as described in 4.2.2.5.

heading: 4.2.3.3 RS-FEC decoding
text:
4.2.3.3 RS-FEC decoding
The PCS Receive function shall check the integrity of the RS-FEC parity bits defined in 4.2.2.4. If the correction
fails, the RS-FEC frame is invalid. Statistics shall be kept in the registers described in 3.2.16 and 3.2.13.
For SG1 and SG2, only the integrity check is mandatory, the correction is optional. If parity is only checked, but
no bit errors are corrected, an RS-FEC frame failing the parity check is also invalid.

A startup PhaseSGB burst txSGB_Up or txSGB_Dn is a concatenation of a single resynchronization
header as defined in 4.2.2.3 and physical layer blocks as defined in 4.2.2.4 as in normal mode TDD
(4.2.2.2) with two differences: firstly, the input data to the physical layer block coding d_plp_tx<7:0>
is equal to zero except for the last physical layer block in each burst (see below). Secondly, the
number of containers per burst in Table 4-2 is replaced by:
Dn Speed Grade

The first bit being sent of the resynchronization header is its LSB. The first bit being sent of the
physical layer block (except the last one) is its MSB. The first bit being sent of the last physical layer
block is its LSB.
The number of symbols in the quiet gap is the same as in normal mode (see Table 4-4).
The last physical layer block is identical to PhaseSGA as defined in Equation 4-12, Equation 4-13 and

heading: 4.2.7.4 Startup PhaseSGC
text:
4.2.7.4 Startup PhaseSGC
A startup PhaseSGC burst txSGC_Up or txSGC_Dn is a concatenation of a single resynchronization
header as defined in 4.2.2.3 and physical layer blocks as defined in 4.2.2.4 as in normal mode TDD
(4.2.2.2) with one difference: the input data to the physical layer block coding d_plp_tx<7:0> is equal
to zero except for the last physical layer block in each burst (see below).
The first bit being sent of the resynchronization header is its LSB. The first bit being sent of the
physical layer block (except the last one) is its MSB. The first bit being sent of the last physical layer
block is its LSB.
The number of symbols in the quiet gap is the same as in normal mode (see Table 4-4).
The last physical layer block is identical to PhaseSGA as defined in Equation 4-13 and Equation 4-14.
The PCS Scrambler is being run as described in 4.2.2.5.2 for Downstream Speed Grades 4 and 5, and
as described in 4.2.2.5.3 for all Upstream Speed Grades.
For Speed Grades 4 and 5 Downstream, scrambled physical layer block symbols and symbols of
Equation 4-13 are mapped to PAM4 as in normal mode (4.2.2.7), scrambled symbols of all Upstream
Speed Grades are mapped to PAM2 as in normal mode (4.2.2.6).

heading: 4.2.8 Precision Time Base
text:
4.2.8 Precision Time Base
Every ASA node has a logical clock PTBclk (see 3.3.19) with a resolution of 4 ns (called a PTB tic). An
ASA node is either a (local) clock leader or a clock follower. There is only one SerDes Branch global
clock leader, which is always the root node.
Coarse synchronization of the follower’s PTBclk is achieved through an info field in the OAM header
from the root node (see 5.5).
Fine synchronization of the follower’s PTBclk is achieved throughcommunication between (local)
clock leader and clock follower on a single point to point connection, where the coding of
Follow/DelayRequest/DelayReply into the resync header is described in 4.2.2.3.5.
The semantics and calculations for both message types are described in the remainder of this section
0.
The clock leader controls the sequence of follow and delay reply messages, Delay Request is always
sent by the follower and does not require an immediate Delay Reply. The clock leader shall at least
send one Follow message between two Delay Reply messages. The clock leader shall send a
minimum of one Delay Reply message for every 15 follow messages.
INFORMATIVE: a ratio of 7 Follow messages to 1 Delay Reply message is recommended.
Local clock leaders copy the PTBclk of the clock follower in the same ASA device once the clock
follower is locked. The definition of the lock state reflected in 3.3.20 is described in 4.2.8.4 in detail.
The deviation of PTBclk in the clock leader(s) and the clock follower in the same device shall never
exceed one PTB tic when clock follower is in locked state.
The clock follower shall achieve a PTBlock condition within 100 TDD cycles after the “PTB initial copy”
(see section 4.2.8.3.1.1) and the recommended ratio of 7 Follow messages to 1 Delay Reply message.

heading: 4.2.8.1.1 Status
text:
4.2.8.1.1 Status
Valid bit in each message can be used to invalidate the message to prevent the follower from using
the time stamps for any calculation.
The local clock leader shall invalidate the status, when the clock follower in the same device is not
locked (status of clock follower is 0).

heading: 4.2.8.1.2 Follow
text:
4.2.8.1.2 Follow
For the Follow message, the time stamp is identical to the lower 14 bits of PTBclk (see 3.3.19) at the
instant, when the first symbol of the first physical layer block of this TDD burst being sent will pass
the local MDI.
If PTBclk is not locked or not running, the time stamp is undefined.

heading: 4.2.8.1.3 Delay Reply
text:
4.2.8.1.3 Delay Reply
For the Delay Reply message, the time stamp is identical to the lower 14 bits of PTBclk (see 3.3.19) at
the instant, when the first symbol of the first physical layer block of the last TDD burst received
passed the local MDI.

heading: 4.2.8.2 Clock Follower Messages
text: 4.2.8.2 Clock Follower Messages

heading: 4.2.8.2.1 Delay Request
text:
4.2.8.2.1 Delay Request
Clock follower only sends back Delay Request messages. This is not explicitly coded since there is no
other message from the clock follower.
For the Delay Request message, the time stamp is identical to the lower 14 bits of PTBclk (see 3.3.19)
at the instant, when the first symbol of the first physical layer block of this TDD burst being sent will
pass the local MDI.This time stamp is also kept in the Clock Follower as “t_PTB_tx” (see4.2.8.3.3).
If PTBclk is not locked or not running, the time stamp is undefined.
Status indicates that follower is locked and time stamp is good. See 4.2.8.4 for a detailed description
of the lock state.
INFORMATIVE: The Delay Request messages time stamp is not required by the clock leader for any
calculation. However, it can be used to sanity check the status being provided.

On the reception of an OAM frame, if the local PTB is unlocked, the PTBclk register (see 3.3.19) is

If the local PTB is locked, the time stamp in the OAM header is used to calculate the PTBoamDly (see

heading: 4.2.9 CRC32
text:
4.2.9 CRC32
The cyclic redundancy check shall use the polynomial 0xF4ACFB13.
The starting value of the CRC is 0xFFFFFFFF.
The appendix (XOR value) of the CRC is 0xFFFFFFFF.
The input data shall be used byte-wise reflected.
The result data shall be used reflected.

heading: 4.3.1 Interburst Gap
text:
4.3.1 Interburst Gap
The nominal Interburst Gap, where neither Upstream nor Downstream transmitter is driving the line,
is equal to 104 ns.

heading: 4.3.2.1 PMA Reset Function
text:
4.3.2.1 PMA Reset Function
The PMA reset function resets all PAM functions and puts the PAM transmit function into
PMA.disable. PMA reset is triggered in Power-On state.

heading: 4.3.2.2.1 PMA.disable
text:
4.3.2.2.1 PMA.disable
PMA.disable is controlled by the PCS according to startup state, TDD state or Light Sleep state. During
disable, 4.4.2.7 shall be fulfilled.

heading: 4.3.2.3 PMA Receive Function
text:
4.3.2.3 PMA Receive Function
The PMA receive function contains circuitry to decode a PAM2 or PAM4 mapping (depending on
Speed Grade) and present the received sequences to the PCS. The quality of these sequences shall be
better than a BER of 10-12after RS-FEC decoding when received from a transmitter according to 4.4.2
over a channel according to 4.5.
INFORMATIVE: The PMA receive function is assumed to operate under thermal noise floor of a
maximum of -160dBm/Hz.

heading: 4.3.2.4 Clock Recovery Function
text:
4.3.2.4 Clock Recovery Function
The clock recovery function is expected to provide a sufficiently stable baud rate clock for sampling
the symbols with the quality described in 4.3.2.3.

heading: 4.3.3.1 Startup State Diagrams
text:
4.3.3.1 Startup State Diagrams
Every ASA node goes through startup Phase1G, PhaseSGA and PhaseSGB. Speed Grades 4 and 5 also
go through startup PhaseSGC. This section contains state diagrams and relevant constants, variables,
timers, counters, functions and messages for the states diagrams.
The patterns for the startup are defined in 4.2.7.
In this entire section 4.3.3.1: when the term root node (leaf node) is used, it is also applicable to any
far-side (near-side) node in an ASA SerDes Branch.
Each node during startup shall not start transmission of a startup burst while a startup burst from the
other side is still being received.

See 1.2.

heading: 4.3.3.1.4 Timers
text:
4.3.3.1.4 Timers
ph1G_root_rx_timer: Timer that is started on the last symbol of Phase1G pattern transmission
from root on the MDI with 200µs, and is stopped on the first symbol of a
successfully received pattern. When the timer reaches zero,
ph1G_root_rx_timer_done = TRUE. An undecodable info field is treated as
an expired timer.
ph1G_leaf_rx_timer: Timer that is started on the last symbol of Phase1G pattern transmission
from leaf on the MDI (or after resetting/modifying ph1G_retry_cnt) with
200µs, and is stopped on the first symbol of a successfully received
pattern. When the timer reaches zero, ph1G_leaf_rx_timer_done = TRUE.
An undecodable info field is treated as an expired timer.
phSGA_root_rx_timer: Timer that is started on the last symbol of PhaseSGA pattern transmission
from root on the MDI with 312ns, and is stopped on the first symbol of a
successfully received pattern. When the timer reaches zero,
phSGA_root_rx_timer_done = TRUE.
In case of a detected signal before expiration of the timer, but an
undecodable infofield, it is up to the implementation to either:
- Keep going and respond with status “TRAINING”
- Go to the FAIL_SGA_1 state to recommence the startup
phSGA_leaf_rx_timer: Timer that is started on the last symbol of PhaseSGA pattern transmission
from leaf on the MDI with 312ns, and is stopped on the first symbol of a
successfully received pattern. When the timer reaches zero,
phSGA_leaf_rx_timer_done = TRUE.
In case of a detected signal before expiration of the timer, but an
undecodable infofield, it is up to the implementation to either:
- Keep going and respond with status “TRAINING”
- Go to the FAIL_SGA_2 state to recommence the startup
phSGB_root_rx_timer: Timer that is started on the last symbol of PhaseSGB pattern transmission
from root on the MDI with 312ns, and is stopped on the first symbol of a
successfully received pattern. When the timer reaches zero,
phSGB_root_rx_timer_done = TRUE.
In case of a detected signal before expiration of the timer, but an
undecodable infofield, it is up to the implementation to either:
- Keep going and respond with status “TRAINING”
- Go to the FAIL_SGB_1 state to recommence the startup
phSGB_leaf_rx_timer: Timer that is started on the last symbol of PhaseSGB pattern transmission
from leaf on the MDI with 312ns, and is stopped on the first symbol of a
successfully received pattern. When the timer reaches zero,
phSGB_leaf_rx_timer_done = TRUE.
In case of a detected signal before expiration of the timer, but an
undecodable infofield, it is up to the implementation to either:
- Keep going and respond with status “TRAINING”
- Go to the FAIL_SGB_2 state to recommence the startup
phSGC_root_rx_timer: Timer that is started on the last symbol of PhaseSGC pattern transmission
from root on the MDI with 312ns, and is stopped on the first symbol of a
successfully received pattern. When the timer reaches zero,
phSGC_root_rx_timer_done = TRUE.
In case of a detected signal before expiration of the timer, but an
undecodable infofield, it is up to the implementation to either:
- Keep going and respond with status “TRAINING”
- Go to the FAIL_SGC_1 state to recommence the startup
phSGC_leaf_rx_timer: Timer that is started on the last symbol of PhaseSGC pattern transmission
from leaf on the MDI with 312ns, and is stopped on the first symbol of a
successfully received pattern. When the timer reaches zero,
phSGC_leaf_rx_timer_done = TRUE.
In case of a detected signal before expiration of the timer, but an
undecodable infofield, it is up to the implementation to either:
- Keep going and respond with status “TRAINING”
- Go to the FAIL_SGC_2 state to recommence the startup
ph1G_leaf_tx_test_timer: Timer that is triggered after loading test pattern and is started with 20ms.
When the timer reaches zero, ph1G_leaf_tx_test_timer_done = TRUE.
ph1G_root_tx_test_timer: Timer that is triggered after sending a test command and is started with
20ms plus inline runtime of respective triggered test (see section 4.4.1.1).
When the timer reaches zero, ph1G_root_tx_test_timer_done = TRUE.
phSGA_leaf_rx_test_timer1: Timer that is triggered after receiving test command and is started
with 20ms. When the timer reaches zero,
phSGA_leaf_rx_test_timer1_done = TRUE.
phSGA_leaf_rx_test_timer2: Timer that is triggered after stopping bit error tester and is started
with 20ms. When the timer reaches zero,
phSGA_leaf_rx_test_timer2_done = TRUE.
phSGA_root_rx_test_timer: Timer that is triggered after test command and is started with the
sum of phSGA_leaf_rx_test_timer1 and phSGA_leaf_rx_test_timer2 plus
inline runtime of respective triggered test (see section 4.4.1.2). When the
timer reaches zero, phSGA_root_rx_test_timer_done = TRUE.

heading: 4.3.3.1.5 Counters
text:

heading: 4.4.1 Test Modes
text:
4.4.1 Test Modes
All Transmitter and Receiver test modes can be triggered by (locally) writing to the register described
in 3.2.18 or by using the command in the respective info field of the startup (see 4.2.7). A test
initiated by writing the register is active until the register value is changed; a test initiated through
the startup info field is only active and non-interactive for a limited time, after which the device
under test cycles back to startup initialization (see 4.3.3.1). The duration to stay in the test is defined
separately for each test mode.
The S11 Termination test can only be activated by (locally) writing the register.

heading: 4.4.1.1 Transmitter Tests
text:
4.4.1.1 Transmitter Tests
All transmitter tests have to be passed at the respective nominal amplitude of the target Speed
Grade.

The pattern shall be recorded 16 times for the linear fit of the pulse response and oversampled with

The transmitter SNDR, shall exceed 38dB in SG5 and SG4, and 32dB in SG3, and 30dB in SG2, and
28dB for SG1. (Note: The values are chosen to limit SNR loss less than 1dB due to TX Nonlinearity.)
For SG4 and 5, a test pattern PRBS13Q is used to do the linearity test for PAM4 signaling, and the
PRBS13Q pattern is defined in 4.4.1.1.2.1. For SG1, SG2 and SG3, a test pattern of PRBS9 is used to
do the linearity test for PAM2 signaling, and the PRBS9 pattern is defined at 4.2.2.3.4.
The full pattern is repeated 128 times, when triggered via startup.

text:
4.4.1.1.2.1 Test Pattern PRBS13Q
The PRBS13Q test pattern is a repeating 8191-symbol sequence formed by Gray coding pairs of bits
from two repetitions of the PRBS13 pattern into PAM4 symbols.

Figure 4-30: PRBS13 pattern generator
The PRBS pattern generator produces the same result as the implementation shown in Figure 4-30,
which implements the generator polynomial shown in Equation 4-18. Since the PRBS13 pattern is an
odd number of bits in length, bits which are mapped as the first bit of a PAM4 symbol during one
repetition of the PRBS13 sequence are mapped as the second bit of a PAM4 symbol during the next
repetition of the PRBS13 sequence, and bits which are mapped as the second bit of a PAM4 symbol
are mapped as the first bit of the following symbol in the next repetition of the PRBS13 sequence.
For example, if the PRBS13 generator used to create the PRBS13Q sequence is initialized to a seed
value of 0010010101010 (with the leftmost bit in S [0] and the rightmost in S[12]), the PRBS13Q

one complete cycle of the PRBS13Q test pattern.

text:
4.4.1.1.3 Jitter Test
The transmit jitter is measured at MDI. The jitter is measured when in using test fixture 2 as shown in
Figure 4-28. When in jitter test mode, the PHY shall transmit a continuous pattern of 16× S {+1}
symbols followed by 16 × S {–1} symbols with the transmitted symbols timed from its local clock
source to have the square wave pattern (‘01’) for all speed grades. SeeTable 4-22 for the definition
of S.

Table 4-22: Speed Grade mapping to S for transmitter test modes
The peak-to-peak value of the MDI output jitter relative to an un-jittered reference is measured. The
band-pass bandwidth of the measurement device shall be larger than 200MHz. The un-jittered
reference is a constant clock frequency extracted from each record of captured differential output on
MDI. The un-jittered reference is based on linear regression of frequency and phase that produces
minimum Time Interval Error. TX Jitter shall be measured over an interval of 1.26us ± 10%, and be
measured 50 times, in none of these time records, the phase drift is allowed to exceed a peak-to-
peak jitter specified in 4.4.2.
The pattern is run for 100 ms, when triggered via startup.

heading: 4.4.1.1.4 Droop Test
text:
4.4.1.1.4 Droop Test
With the transmitter in droop test and using the transmitter test fixture 1 shown in Figure 4-28.
When in droop test, the PHY shall transmit a continuous pattern of 160 × S {+1} symbols followed by
160 × S {–1} symbols with the transmitted symbols timed from its local clock source. See Table 4-22
for the definition of S. The magnitude of both the positive and negative droop shall be less than 32%
measured with respect to an initial value at 4 ns after the zero crossing and a final value at 16 ns
after the zero crossing (12 ns period).
The pattern is run for 10 ms, when triggered via startup.

heading: 4.4.1.1.5 PSD Test
text:
4.4.1.1.5 PSD Test
PSD test is for checking whether the transmitter is compliant with the transmit PSD masks that are
defined in 4.4.2. In this test mode, the transmitter is at normal operations at the relative speed
grade, the transmit power measured into a 100 Ω load using the test fixture 2 shownin Figure 4-29.
The pattern is run for 500 ms, when triggered via startup.

heading: 4.4.1.1.6 BER Test
text:
4.4.1.1.6 BER Test
For BER test, the transmitter is operating as in Normal Mode on PCS/PMA at the relative speed
grade, the transmitted pattern is measured in a capturing device using the test fixture 1 shown in
Figure 4-28.
All the d_plp_tx are set to zero and the side stream scrambler is started with seed 0x700000.
The pattern is run for 500 ms, when triggered via startup.

text:
4.4.1.2.2 BER Test
This test mode operates the same way as noise immunity test, but runs for 500 ms when triggered

heading: 4.4.1.3 S11 Termination Test
text:
4.4.1.3 S11 Termination Test
For S11 testing, the transceiver shall present the normal data mode termination to the PMD interface
while the transmitter is disabled. See also 3.2.18.
This test can only be triggered through local ASA register access.

heading: 4.4.1.4 Phase1G Loopback Test
text:
4.4.1.4 Phase1G Loopback Test
For this test mode, the device acts as a root node for PCS/PAM transmit and a non-root node for
PCS/PMA receive. The detection of a single Phase1G block is signaled by setting Polarity Detect in the
register defined in 3.2.12 to 0x01 and concludes the test.
This test can only be triggered through local ASA register access.

heading: 4.4.2 Transmitter Electrical Specification
text: 4.4.2 Transmitter Electrical Specification

heading: 4.4.2.1 Support of cable types
text:
4.4.2.1 Support of cable types
The transmitter in every speed grade supports an STP cable with a nominal 100Ω impedance and a
coax cable with a nominal impedance of 50Ω.
If not explicitly denoted, the electrical specifications in the section refer to STP cable. The
corresponding values for coax cables obtained by adjusting the value to 50% of the amplitude in Volt
or -3dB for dBm respectively.

heading: 4.4.2.2.1 Transmitter peak output
text:
4.4.2.2.1 Transmitter peak output
With MDI for STP terminated by 100Ω, the differential nominal amplitude at the MDI shall be 0.7V
peak-to-peak.
With MDI for Coax terminated by 50Ω, the nominal amplitude at the MDI shall be 0.35V peak-to-
peak.

PLP_TX.dataUnit(d_plp_tx<7:0><0:len-1>)

Phase1G sequence is reached (near-side node).

heading: 4.7.1.3.3 Effect of receipt
text:
4.7.1.3.3 Effect of receipt
Link Aggregation Sublayer (optional)
The Link Aggregation Sublayer defines sublayer between PCS and DLL, which maps Physical Layer
Port Primitives between a single port on the DLL side to multiple ports on the PCS side. Its
implementation is optional.

heading: 4.8.1 Overview

figures.title: Link Aggregation Sublayer in the stacks of a point-to-point connection

text:
4.8.1 Overview
The Link Aggregation Sublayer allows the aggregation of the communication over 2-4 physical layer
ports into a single physical layer port.
The Link aggregation Sublayer shall only aggregate physical layers of identical Speed Grades and
direction (Downstream or Upstream). This limitation preserves the order of physical layer blocks (and
DLL containers).
Informative: differential delay due to different propagation delay on the cable can be compensated
in the receiver. The combination of minimum and maximum channel length is allowed, see also
section 4.5).
There shall only be a single DLL instance in the presence of a Link Aggregation Sublayer.
There is only a single instance of PTBclk (see section 3.3.19 and 0). Also refer to section 4.8.3.

heading: 4.8.3 PTB Function for Link Aggregation
text:
4.8.3 PTB Function for Link Aggregation
The PTB Clock Leader and PTB Clock Follower shall exchange messages (see section 0), which are
used to update the PTBclk, only via lowest LinkID in use.
All other lanes shall repeat the Follow message (Clock Leader) or Delay Request message (clock
follower).
Informative: The PTB time stamps in these messages can be used to update latency compensation.

heading: 4.8.4 Startup Behavior for Link Aggregation
text:
4.8.4 Startup Behavior for Link Aggregation
In a Link Aggregation configuration, the Startup procedure synchronizes the half-duplex TDD cycles
between Lanes, see section 4.3.3.1.
In addition, the Physical Layers shall use the flexibility of the timeout period of Startup phases SGA,
SGB and SGC to achieve a staggered start of their transmitted Downstream/Upstream bursts, such
that the relative delay between the first symbol of the burst passing the local MDI of the Lanes is
(measured in line rate symbols):
Lane0 … 0 symbols,
Lane1 … 64 symbols,
Lane2 … 128 symbols,
Lane3 … 192 symbols.
Informative: This stagger avoids the concurrent transmission of resynchronization headers.

heading: 4.8.4.1 Handling of LinkID and GroupID
text:
4.8.4.1 Handling of LinkID and GroupID
LinkID and GroupID are exchanged in the m_ptb field of Startup Phase1G, see section 4.2.7.1.
The Root node (or far-side node) defines the linkID (sending the value from register in section
3.2.19); The Leaf node (or near-side node) copies the received value into the same register.
The Leaf node replies with same LinkID for confirmation; replies with differing linkID to indicate error
(see register in section 3.2.19).
The Root node (or far-side node) sends the GroupID (equal to value in register in section 3.2.2) on all
links. The Leaf node (or near-side node) responds with the GroupID received on the lowest linkID on
all links.
The Root node checks the received GroupID values and reports the status in the register in section
3.2.4.

heading: 4.8.5 Individual Status and Control
text:
4.8.5 Individual Status and Control
Each link shall update its own separate status in registers 3.2.12 through 3.2.17 and allow individual
test control by means of register 3.2.18 or their respective register map ranges (see section 3.2).

heading: 4.8.6 Error Handling
text:
4.8.6 Error Handling
A link fail (unrecoverable link loss) on one of the aggregated links shall immediately lead to a Fail
state (see section 2.4) for the entire node.

The Data Link Layer interfaces to the Physical Layer via PLP_TX and PLP_RX, and interfaces to the
Application Stream Encapsulator/Decapsulator via DLP_TX and DLP_RX.
It contains two functional sub-blocks: the OAM entity and Security entity. The OAM entity uses the
interfaces DLP_TX and DLP_RX as well. The Security entity defines its own interfaces.
There is only a single PLP_TX and single PLP_RX connected to a Data Link Layer. There are up to 64
DLP_TX and up to 64 DLP_RX connected to a DLL, which are identified by their respective DLP_TX_ID
and DLP_RX_ID. OAM is by definition connected to DLP_TX_ID=0 and DLP_RX_ID=0.

heading: 5.1.1 Data Link Layer Functions
text:
5.1.1 Data Link Layer Functions
The Data Link Layer provides the means to transport fixed size Data Link Layer Containers from one
node to one or more nodes in the SerDes Branch.
The payload of any Data Link Layer Container is provided to the Data Link Layer at the DLP_TX and is
delivered to OAM/ASD/FoFa at the DLP_RX.
The Data Link Layer is handling the Multiplexing of Data Link Layer Containers onto the PLP_TX and
the Demultiplexing from the PLP_RX onto the appropriate DLP_RXs. Demultiplexing includes
Duplication of multicast containers, when applicable.
The Multiplexing includes a Scheduling (deterministic time slot mapping) functionality.

heading: 5.2.1 Data Link Layer Transmit Process
text:
5.2.1 Data Link Layer Transmit Process
The Transmit Process in the DLL is cyclic with the occurrence of a physical layer block in the PCS
Transmit Process.
The following steps are executed (in the listed order), when DLL is triggered by 4.6.1.2:
a) Evaluation Step of the Mapper (see 5.2.3.3), which yields a DLP_TX_ID_toSend
b) That DLP_TX_ID is polled with primitive DLP_TX.indicateSlot (see 5.6.1.1)
c) Wait for a response on DLP with DLP_TX_ID
d) Construct container header, also depending on primitive replied (see 5.2.2)
e) If security is enabled:
1. Call primitive in LLS (see 6.3.2.1)
2. Wait for LLS to respond
i. In case of 6.3.2.2, continue with f)
ii. In case of 6.3.2.5, call 4.6.1.1 with an array of all zeros
f) Put DLL container to PLP_TX (see 4.6.1.1) while bit order inside bytes is the same (i.e.
d_plp_tx<7>,<0> is the MSB of the first byte of the DLL container header)

heading: 5.2.3 Mapping/Multiplexing
text:
5.2.3 Mapping/Multiplexing
The Mapper provides the mechanism for a time-division access of a multitude of DLP_TX (one OAM
and one or more Application Stream Encapsulators and/or Forwarding Fabrics) onto the PLP_TX
(Physical Layer). The Mapper is configurable via ASA registers, which determine the length and
contents of one Mapper Cycle. The Mapper Cycle is a sequence of DLP_TX_IDs that represent the
allocation of container slots to these DLP_TX_IDs.

heading: 5.2.3.1 Configurability
text:
5.2.3.1 Configurability
The data object for the mapper operation are all accessible through the register map:
Counter (see 3.3.8)
CounterMin (see 3.3.9)
CounterMax (see 3.3.10)
LineMin (see 3.3.11)
LineMax (see 3.3.12)
MapperTable (see 3.3.13)
The length of the Mapper cycle is “CounterMax-CounterMin+1”.
The MapperTable determines the sequence of DLP_TX_ID in the Mapper Cycle. LineMin and LineMax
function as indexing pointers into the MapperTable to select a consecutive block of lines to evaluate.

heading: 5.2.3.2 Mapper Initialization
text:
5.2.3.2 Mapper Initialization
At initialization, the Counter is set to CounterMin.

heading: 5.2.3.3 Mapper Evaluation Step
text:
5.2.3.3 Mapper Evaluation Step
The evaluation step is executed for each container transmit opportunity. This section is a description
of a mandatory functional behavior based on the configured register values. However, it does not
mandate an implementation.
LINE is a combination of three consecutive registers holding BitMask, CompareValue,
DLP_TX_ID_toSend as illustrated in Table 3-46.
LINES is an ordered subset of Table 3-46.
Starting with first LINE, the Counter is bit-wise AND-concatenated and the result is compared to
CompareValue. If the comparison yields FALSE, the next LINE is tried. If the comparison yields TRUE,
the DLP_TX_ID to be sent has been found in that LINE and the remainder of LINES is not evaluated.
Lastly, the Counter is incremented and it is checked, whether it exceeds its range. If this is the case, it
is reset to CounterMin.
If no LINE has evaluated TRUE, the default value DLP_TX_ID=0 (OAM) is used.
Figure 5-4 shows pseudo-code illustrating the Initialization and Evaluation Step.

LINES = MapperTable[LineMin:LineMax]
Evaluation Step

LINE_sel = (Counter&&LINE.BitMask == LINE.CompareValue) ? 1 : 0
if (LINE_sel == 1) breakloop
DLP_TX_ID_select = LINE.DLP_TX_ID_toSend
Counter++
if (Counter > CounterMax) then Counter = CounterMin

heading: 5.3.1 Data Link Layer Receive Process
text:
5.3.1 Data Link Layer Receive Process
When PLP_RX is active, the DLL takes received data container by container triggered by 4.7.1.1. For
each container, the following steps are executed:
a) If security is enabled
1. Call primitive 6.3.2.3
2. Wait for LLS to respond
i. In case of 6.3.2.4, execute b)
ii. In case of 6.3.2.5, wait for next container on PLP_RX
b) Execute the cases in 5.3.2 with the values from the current container header

heading: 5.5 OAM
text:
OAM
Operation, Administration, Management is an ASA internal communication channel between the
root node and the non-root nodes in Branch and Leaf Devices. The root node runs an OAM session
with each non-root node whereas each non-root node only runs a single OAM session with the root
node.
OAM is used to configure and control ASA nodes and to obtain status and diagnostics/debug
information of ASA nodes, both through OAM CAD (Command-Address-Data) for access of the ASA
register map and complementing special instructions.
LongAtom is a special OAM mechanism, in which a marked block of CAD operations spanning more
than one OAM frame are buffered at the receiving side and only executed, when the LongAtomClose
is received.
If Security is present, OAM is also used to facilitate communication with the Key Exchange Entity.

status of PTB and a short list of mandatory and implementer-defined link health registers. The
header also contains a CADnext flag to signal, whether there is a command present after the header.
The MSB in the first byte of any CAD indicates, whether there is an additional CAD present.

INFORMATIVE: OAMerror supports debug of OAM communication problems; it does not support
high robustness of communication under error condition

The OAM transmit and receive is linked to the DLL Transmit Process (see 5.2.1) and the DLL Receive

of CADs, response to CADs and error handling is described in 5.5.3.

5.5.3 Command-Address-Data
Every CAD structure starts with the Command byte:
Byte Bit(s) Name | Description
n | CADnext | 1: further CAD present after this CAD, 0: no
further CAD present

The additional fields Address and Data are defined per command below. Addresses refer to ASA
register addresses (see 3). Data refers to any parameters/values passed on with the command.
The commands are coded with 7 bits:

…

heading: 5.5.3.7 LongAtom

tables.title: LongAtom Command Address-Data

text:
5.5.3.7 LongAtom
There is no Address or Data for this command. This command signals (at the end of an OAM frame),
that the Write commands contained in this frame shall be buffered and only written, when a
LongAtomClose command is received. Each OAM frame before the LongAtomClose shall contain a
LongAtom CAD (at the end of an OAM frame).
Byte Bit(s) Name | Description
n+1 7:5 | reserved
n+1 4:0 | LongAtom OAM frame first frame of each LongAtom starts with 0, each
counter | successive frame of same LongAtom increments
the counter by 1
Table 5-12: LongAtom Command Address-Data
Between LongAtom and LongAtomClose, only Write commands are allowed. The maximum number
of consecutive LongAtom marked OAM frames are is limited to 31. No non-LongAtom OAM frames
containing CADs are allowed to be inserted between LongAtom and LongAtomClose (it is allowed to
intersperse empty OAM frames, containing just the OAM header, between LongAtom and
LongAtomClose). The 32ndframe must contain a LongAtomClose. If the LongAtomClose is not
received in the 32ndframe or one OAM frame up to the LongAtomClose was corrupted or is missing,
the Leaf must respond with all WriteAck = “Write fail”.
INFORMATIVE: This limit allows the atomic programming of the Mapper table including some
headroom through the upstream channel.

heading: 5.5.4 Startup Enumeration Procedure
text:
5.5.4 Startup Enumeration Procedure
Enumeration, i.e. the distribution of addresses/nodeIDs in the SerDes Branch, is initiated by the root
node with Node-Discover (see 5.5.4.1) messages.
Node-Discover messages use extended headers for multi-cast, which do not occur in normal mode
OAM operation.
By means of Self-Announce (see 5.5.4.2) messages, the root node receives the information, how
many forwarding DLP are present (which implies how many nodes are implemented in the same
device).
After the root node receives a Self-Announce, it can address normal OAM messages explicitly to this
newnode and configure DLP_TX with ASEP stream type “Return OAM”and “Forward Data”(see
Table 7-1) for a slot in the mapper table (see 0) and an entry in the addressing table (see 3.3.6).
Deterministic one-by-one Forwarding of Node-Discover messages is ensured by the Data Link Layer
Receive Process (see 5.3). Far-side nodes can be directly addressed with OAM messages after the
near side Demultiplexing Table 2 (see 3.3.16) has been updated by the root node.
To the far-side node, the root can now send OAM messages to configure DLP_TX with ASEP stream
type “Forward Data” (seeTable 7-1) for a slot in the mapper table (see 0) and an entry in the
addressing table (see 3.3.6).
The enumeration is continued further out behind this far-side node by sending a Node-Discover
message with one targetID equal to the far-side nodeID and one targetID=0.
It is the responsibility of the root node to update the Demultiplexing Table 2 (see 3.3.16) in
previously enumerated nodes to list the nodeIDs of newly discovered nodes in the topology.

heading: 5.5.4.1.1 Generation
text:
5.5.4.1.1 Generation
This message is sent by the root node.
The HeaderType is set to 1, the targetID0 for the container of this OAM frame is set to 0, the
targetID1 is set to that near-side nodeID, behind which further nodes need to be discovered.
CADnext is set to 1, OAMerror is set to 0 (see Table 5-2).
OAMframeID is started with 0, but incremented for every OAM frame with the same set of targetIDs.
There is a single StartEnum command (see 5.5.3.6) in the frame carrying the next (currently still
unused) nodeID for enumeration.

heading: 5.5.4.1.2 Effect of receipt
text:
5.5.4.1.2 Effect of receipt
Receiving node OAM entity writes the nodeID to local register (see 3.3.1) and replies with Self-
Announce (see 5.5.4.2).

heading: 5.5.4.2.1 Generation
text:
5.5.4.2.1 Generation
This is the reply to a received Node-Discover (see 5.5.4.1).
The HeaderType is set to 1, the targetID0 for the container of this OAM frame is set to 1, all other
targetIDs are set to 0.
CADnext is set to 1, OAMerror is set to 0 (see Table 5-2).
The reception of a Node-Discover not matching specification leads to a Self-announce with:
OAMerror is set to 0x3.
OAMframeID is started with 0, but incremented for every OAM frame with targetID=1.
The OAM frame contains Return commands (see 5.5.3.2) for the following registers:
DLLconfig1 (see 3.3.2)
DLLconfig2 (see 3.3.3)
VendorID (see 3.3.4)
DeviceID (see 3.3.5)
ASEP Stream Type (see 3.5.1.2) for all supported/enabled DLPs

heading: 5.5.4.2.2 Effect of receipt
text:
5.5.4.2.2 Effect of receipt
Root node reacts with further OAM messages to origin nodeID for additional configuration as
appropriate.

section_title: Data Link Layer Port Transmit Interface
heading: 5.6 Data Link Layer Port Transmit Interface
text: Data Link Layer Port Transmit Interface

heading: 5.6.1 Primitives
text:
5.6.1 Primitives
The primitives in this section are used during the Data Link Layer Transmit Process (see 5.2.1) for
communication between DLL Transmit Process, OAM (see 5.5) and Application Stream Encapsulator
(see 7.1).

heading: 5.6.1.1.1 Semantics of the primitive
text:
5.6.1.1.1 Semantics of the primitive
DLP_TX.indicateSlot(size)
The DLL uses indicateSlot to request from the ASE or OAM respectively a data unit of size to transmit.
The size parameter can take one of the following values:
Dn_P2P | Downstream for point to point stream (638 bytes)
Dn_P2P_Sec | Downstream for point to point stream, secured (620 bytes)
Dn_MC | Downstream for multicast stream (636 bytes)
Dn_MC_Sec | Downstream for multicast stream, secured (618 bytes)
Up_P2P | Upstream for point to point stream (208 bytes)
Up_P2P_Sec | Upstream for point to point stream, secured (190 bytes)
Up_MC | Upstream for multicast stream (206 bytes)
Up_MC_Sec | Upstream for multicast stream, secured (188 bytes)
OAM_frame | Downstream and Upstream, any configuration (188 bytes)

heading: 5.6.1.1.2 When generated
text:
5.6.1.1.2 When generated
DLL generates indicateSlot after each evaluation of the Mapper table for a new transmit opportunity.

heading: 5.6.1.1.3 Effect of receipt
text:
5.6.1.1.3 Effect of receipt
ASE replies with 5.6.1.2 or 5.6.1.4. OAM always replies with 5.6.1.3 (sending at least an OAM frame
header).

heading: 5.6.1.2.1 Semantics of the primitive
text:
5.6.1.2.1 Semantics of the primitive
DLP_TX.dataUnit(ase_payload)
The ASE uses DLP_TX.dataUnit to provide the payload of a container to the DLL. The size shall be the
size, which has been requested.

heading: 5.6.1.2.2 When generated
text:
5.6.1.2.2 When generated
After reception of DLP_TX.indicateSlot (see 5.6.1.1), if payload is available.

heading: 5.6.1.2.3 Effect of receipt
text:
5.6.1.2.3 Effect of receipt
DLL uses the provided ase_payload in the next container to be sent.

heading: 5.6.1.3.1 Semantics of the primitive
text:
5.6.1.3.1 Semantics of the primitive
DLP_TX.oamUnit(oam_payload, targetID, packetID, ndEn, targetIDs)
The OAM uses DLP_TX.oamUnit to provide the payload of a container, the target node identifier and
the packet identifier to the DLL. The size shall be the size, which has been requested. If the OAM
frame uses less bytes than the request size, the OAM shall pad with zeros.
The packetID provided is identical to the lower 5 bits of the OAMframeID (see Table 5-2).
If ndEn=TRUE, the message supplied is a Node-Discover message and targetIDs contains three
additional IDs for an extended header.

heading: 5.6.1.3.2 When generated
text:
5.6.1.3.2 When generated
After reception of DLP_TX.indicateSlot (see 5.6.1.1), if payload is available.

heading: 5.6.1.3.3 Effect of receipt
text:
5.6.1.3.3 Effect of receipt
DLL uses the provided oam_payload, targetID and packetID in the next container to be sent.

heading: 5.6.1.4.1 Semantics of the primitive
text:
5.6.1.4.1 Semantics of the primitive
DLP_TX.yield()
The ASE or FoFa uses DLP_TX.yield to signal, that it has no data to send and forfeits the transmit
opportunity.

heading: 5.6.1.4.2 When generated
text:
5.6.1.4.2 When generated
After reception of DLP_TX.indicateSlot (see 5.6.1.1), if no payload is available.

heading: 5.6.1.4.3 Effect of receipt
text:
5.6.1.4.3 Effect of receipt
No container is constructed for this ASE. Instead, OAM is polled with 5.6.1.1.

heading: 5.6.1.5.1 Semantics of the primitive
text:
5.6.1.5.1 Semantics of the primitive
DLP_TX.oamFrameLocal(container, phyLerrStat)
The FoFa uses DLP_TX.oamFrameLocal to signal to the DLL, that it has a container (with an OAM
frame) addressed to the local node. phyLerrStat is equal to errStat in 4.7.1.1.

heading: 5.6.1.5.2 When generated
text:
5.6.1.5.2 When generated
Always, when OAMreturnQueue is not empty and the targetID in the container header is equal to the
local nodeID.

heading: 5.6.1.5.3 Effect of receipt
text:
5.6.1.5.3 Effect of receipt
DLL takes data the same way as from PLP_RX (see 4.7.1.1) and feeds it to the Data Link Layer Receive
Process (see 5.3.1)
If nodeID=0 (see 3.3.1), then DLL copies FoFa ReturnPath (see 3.6.1) onto register OAMdmxTX (see
0).

heading: 5.6.1.6.1 Semantics of the primitive
text:
5.6.1.6.1 Semantics of the primitive
DLP_TX.forwardUnit(size, header, payload)
The FoFa uses DLP_TX.forwardUnit to provide the header and the payload of a container to the DLL.

Light Sleep
The support of Light Sleep feature is optional.
Light Sleep enables duty cycling of the traffic of the link on a time scale of a sensor or display cycle, it
can stop traffic on the link for up to 4096 TDD cycles (or nominally 112,132,096ns) and has a
minimum lower boundary for the time to go to Light Sleep. That minimum boundary is mediated by
the root node for every Light Sleep event.
INFORMATIVE: The minimum sleep time lies in the order of 250µs.
The Light Sleep state
- Stops Mapper, extends the quiet gap
- PMA TX and RX are disabled
All other functions of Normal Mode remain on, especially PTBclk is required to keep running on a
local reference.
During Light Sleep, the PTBclk is allowed to drift a maximum of 140 PTB tics from its nominal
position.
INFORMATIVE: 140 PTB tics is equal to 560 ns, which is deemed a tolerable search window for a
Phase1G startup pattern length of 3.28µs with a resynchronization header of 384 ns.
Extended Figure 5-11 is purely INFORMATIVE to illustrate a possible use of Light Sleep.

Entering Light Sleep and restarting from Light Sleep follows the TDD half-duplexing granularity and
sequence of startup. This means, on each link participating in Light Sleep, the near-side node sends
the last data burst and the far-side node (or root node itself) sends the first pattern of startup.

heading: 5.8.1 Entering Light Sleep
text:
5.8.1 Entering Light Sleep
Light Sleep is negotiated via exchange of special OAM CADs described in 5.5, whereas state diagrams
are described in 5.8.3.
Light Sleep is announced by either root or a non-root node, but always executed by the root node.
The non-initiating node must deny Light Sleep under certain conditions and always can deny Light
Sleep; no node can be forced into Light Sleep.
It is the responsibility of the root node to mediate the decision to go into Light Sleep including its
parameters of time to sleep and restart time.
This means to announce Light Sleep to all non-initiating nodes, which are affected, either by being on
the same link of the announcing node or by being on a part of the ASA SerDes Branch that is
connected to the root node by the link that wants to go to Light Sleep. Light Sleep shall not isolate a
node in normal mode from the root node.
This also means to determine from all announced or confirmed parameters, whether Light Sleep is
feasible, i.e. a controlled time to enter Light Sleep as well as enough time to restart from sleeping is
available for all affected nodes.
If either of these conditions cannot be met, the root node shall deny Light Sleep.

heading: 5.8.1.1 Check by Non-Root
text:
5.8.1.1 Check by Non-Root
The check by a non-root node for an LSconfirm of Light Sleep has several mandatory conditions,
which need to be met:
- PTB is locked
- SleepCycles*phSGx_TIME - (RestartCycles1G_a*ph1G_TIME +
RestartCyclesSGx_a*phSGx_TIME) > 25,000 … estimation of own sleep time before restart
has to be larger than 100µs
- PTBbedtime–PTBclk > 12,500 … announced time to go to sleep has to be at least 50µs into
the future
- PTB drift during SleepCycles*phSGx_TIME - (RestartCycles1G_a*ph1G_TIME +
RestartCyclesSGx_a*phSGx_TIME) is less than 140 PTB tics
If any of these conditions is not met, Light Sleep shall be denied.
Light Sleep is allowed to be denied any time.

heading: 5.8.1.2 Check by Root
text:
5.8.1.2 Check by Root
The root node shall collect all LSconfirm messages from affected nodes and evaluate the maxima
RestartCycles1G_f=max(RestartCycles1G_a_1, … , RestartCycles1G_a_n) and
RestartCyclesSGx_f=max(RestartCyclesSGx_a_1, … , RestartCyclesSGx_a_n).
Based on these values, the following conditions shall be met:
- PTB is locked
- SleepCycles*phSGx_TIME - (RestartCycles1G_f*ph1G_TIME +
RestartCyclesSGx_f*phSGx_TIME) > 25,000 … estimation of own sleep time beforerestart
has to be larger than 100µs
- PTBbedtime–PTBclk > 12,500 … announced time to go to sleep has to be at least 50µs into
the future
If any of these conditions is not met, LSpossible is FALSE.
Light Sleep is allowed to be denied any time.
PTBalarmclock = PTBbedtime + SleepCycles*phSGx_TIME - (RestartCycles1G_f*ph1G_TIME +
RestartCyclesSGx_f*phSGx_TIME)

DLL Startup, OAM config
After Physical Layer Startup, communication between the root nodes DLL/OAM and the non-root
nodes DLL/OAM can take place.
If the required ASA nodes/devices configurations for Normal Mode are persistently stored beyond a
power cycle (or the device come back from Light Sleep), Normal Mode can be initiated by setting the
appropriate bit in the startup info field (see 4.2.7.5). Informative: The definition of this required
configuration depends on the application context.
If ASA nodes need to be configured, the default values of Addressing Table, Mapper and
Demultiplexing allow establishing communication via the OAM channel with the link partner and to
extended this communication throughout the SerDes Branch. See also section 5.5.4.
In the case of the OAM config state, the transition to Normal Mode is initiated by the StartTDD CAD
(see 5.5.3.9).

heading: 6.2 Keys and IDs

figures.title: Cryptographic Key Overview example (informative)

text:
Security Entity
The existence of the Security Entity is optional.
Normative References for Security:
NIST FIPS PUB 197: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
NIST Special Publication 800-38D: Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation:
Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC
Overview (Informational)
The Security functionality of this standard is made up by two high level components:
•
Key Exchange Entity–which is responsible for handling and exchanging keys. This
component is responsible for storing the keys securely. Key Exchange messages are
transported by the OAM channel.
•
Link Layer Security–which is responsible for protecting messages using keys provided by the
Key Exchange Entity. Protection means authentication and integrity protection. Encryption of
containers is an optional feature.
Keys and IDs
Achieving Security typically requires the use of cryptography, which in case requires cryptographic
keys. Additionally, the identification of devices needs to be defined as well.
Due to limitations regarding excess processing power on small sensors and cameras, only symmetric
cryptography is used. The symmetric keys are used for the AES algorithm (NIST, FIPS PUB 197:
Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)). AES will be used using the GCM or GMAC block mode (NIST,
Special Publication 800-38D: Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter
Mode (GCM) and GMAC).
Based on symmetric cryptography, the Key Hierarchy consists of 3 layers (top to bottom):
•
Device Keys (DK)–the top-level key of an ASA Device.
•
Binding Keys (BK)–the key binding an ASA Device to a vehicle.
•
Link Keys (LK)–session keys for the Link Layer Security, which are shared by adjacent
devices.
These keys are explained in the detail in the following sections.
The identity of an ASA device is based on a 128-bit number, called UUID in this document.
Figure 6-1: Cryptographic Key Overview example (informative)

heading: 6.2.1 General Requirements for Key Length
text:
6.2.1 General Requirements for Key Length
All devices shall support DKs, BKs, and LKs as 128bit AES keys.
All devices may support DKs, BKs, and LKs as 256bit AES keys.
If a device supports a 256bit AES BK, it shall support a 256bit AES DK as well.
If a device supports 256bit AES LKs, it shall support a 256bit AES BK and 256bit AES DK.
Each Device shall keep track of the Lengths of all installed Keys.

heading: 6.2.2 Device Keys
text:
6.2.2 Device Keys
Each ASA Device shall have one symmetric Device Key DK.
A Device Key (DK):
•
should be unique over all devices of an OEM.
•
forms the root of trust between the OEM and the device.
•
and thereby can be used to prevent counterfeit devices.
The device key itself is calculated from two sub-keys:
•
The Device Key Tier-1 part (DK_0) is persistently written to the ASA Device by the Tier1
during ECU production.
•
The Device Key OEM part (DK_1) is persistently written to the ASA Device by the OEM during
car production.
Device Key shall be calculated as a XOR operation of DK_0 and DK_1.
DK_0 and DK_1 shall each have the same size as DK.

heading: 6.3 Link Layer Security
text:
For unwritten Device Keys, 0x00 shall be used as key value.
Device Key sub-keys shall be only one-time writable.
Device Keys and Device Key sub-keys shall not be readable from outside the ASA nodes on the device
(including OAM Channel).

heading: 6.2.3 Binding Keys
text:
6.2.3 Binding Keys
A Binding Key (BK) is binding an ECU to a vehicle to prevent theft parts from functioning in another
vehicle.
Each pair of Root Device (representing the vehicle) and a Non-Root Device connected to the Root
Device shall have one shared Binding Key (BK).
Binding Keys shall be symmetric.
Bindings Keys shall be changeable.
Binding Keys shall support a minimum of 16 write cycles.
A device might break, when installing a binding key more often than designed for.
Binding Keys shall not be readable from outside the ASA nodes on the device (including OAM
Channel).
Binding Keys shall be persistent to a power cycle.

heading: 6.2.4 Link Keys
text:
6.2.4 Link Keys
A Link Key (LK) is used to authenticate, integrity protect, and optionally encrypt messages on an ASA
link between two adjacent devices.
Link Keys shall be symmetric.
Link Keys shall not be stored persistently beyond the power cycle since this might affect overall
security (informative).
Link Keys shall be installed at least once in every power cycle.
Link Keys shall not be readable from outside the ASA nodes on the device (including OAM Channel).

heading: 6.2.5 UUIDs
text:
6.2.5 UUIDs
Each device shall support a one-time writable 128-bit number, called UUID.
If the UUID was not written yet, it shall be 0.
The UUID shall be freely readable.
The structure and mechanisms to make UUIDs unique in an OEMs area of concern, is up to the OEM.
Link Layer Security
The Link Layer Security describes the protection of incoming and outgoing messages.

section_title: General concepts of Link Layer Security Primitives
heading: 6.3.1 General concepts of Link Layer Security Primitives
text:
6.3.1 General concepts of Link Layer Security Primitives
The Link Layer Security shall provide link layer security. That is security between the two nodes on a
single link. This does not include end-to-end security.
The Link Layer Security can be used in two modes:
1. “Authentication Only”mode.
2. “Authentication and Encryption” mode.
While the first mode is required for all devices implementing Security, the second mode is optional.
Informative: Since the overhead of additionally implementing the second mode is very small,
implementing both is strongly recommended.

heading: 6.3.1.1 Link Layer Security Algorithms
text:
6.3.1.1 Link Layer Security Algorithms
Link Layer Security shall support AES-GMAC-128 with 128bit LKs by default.
Link Layer Security should support AES-GCM-128 with 128bit LKs.
Link Layer Security may support AES-GMAC-256 with 256bit LKs.
Link Layer Security may support AES-GCM-256 with 256bit LKs.

heading: 6.3.1.2 Initialization Vector construction

tables.title: Link Layer Security IV Construction

text:
6.3.1.2 Initialization Vector construction
For a given key, the Initialization Vector (IV) for the AEAD algorithm needs to be unique for every
packet protected with it.
The Length of the IV for Link Layer Security based on AES-GCM or AES-GMAC shall be 96 bits.
The IV for Link Layer Security shall consist of a fixed field (32 bit) and an invocation field (64 bit).
Construction:
Part | Field | Length (bit)
KeyEx = 0
Fixed Field (32 bit) | Dir
Salt
Invocation Field (64 bit) | Link Layer TX AEAD Invocation Counter
Table 6-1: Link Layer Security IV Construction
The fields shall be defined as follows:
•
KeyEx: Shall be 0 since the IV belongs to a secured Link Layer Container and not a Key
Exchange message.
•
Dir: Shall be 0 if the secured Link Layer Container is a Downstream Container and 1 if the
secured Link Layer Container is an Upstream Container.
•
Salt: Shall be set by the Link Key Installation (see 6.4.3.12)
“NextLink Layer TX AEAD Invocation Counter”: Counter that increments for every AEAD invocation in
TX direction for secured Link Layer Containers only and starts with 1.

section_title: Format of Container with Security enabled
heading: 6.3.1.3 Format of Container with Security enabled

figures.title: Container Format with Security enabled

text:
6.3.1.3 Format of Container with Security enabled
authentication / integrity check in LLS
payload LLS protection flag | optional encryption in LLS
reserved Counter
Container Header | DLL Payload (secured) | ICV
6:0 (lower byte)
Security Payload
Figure 6-2: Container Format with Security enabled
The Security Entity constructs a Container Payload out of the DLL payload and two additional fields:
Counter and ICV. See also Figure 5-3.
The Container Header HDR contains the bit “KeySwitch” indicating the used key slot(see 5.2.2).
See also section 6.3.4 for handling of these fields during LLS message processing.

heading: 6.3.1.3.1 Counter
text:
6.3.1.3.1 Counter
Length: 8 bits
Relative Position: Between Container Header and Container Payload
The Counter represents the 8 least significant bits of a 64-bit Link Layer TX AEAD Invocation Counter.

heading: 6.3.1.3.2 ICV
text:
6.3.1.3.2 ICV
Length: 128 bits
Relative Position: After Container Payload
The field ICV is the Integrity Check Value of all Container fields starting with the Container Header
and ending with the Container payload.
In case of AES-GCM or AES-GMAC, the ICV is represented by the Auth Tag.

6.3.4.1 LinkLayerSec.process_incoming_message
This process shall handle an incoming container (for DLL receive process, see section 5.3.1) and is
executed after primitive 6.3.2.3 has been called by the DLL.
The following incoming OAM messages shall pass without checks and modifications by the link layer
security and return by primitive 6.3.2.4
•
All OAM frames/messages with KeyEx primitives
•
Enumeration messages:
o Node Discover
o Self Announce
All such incoming OAM messages shall have byte0,bit7=0 (of the Security Payload) to identify them
as unprotected by Link Layer Security.
OAM messages not listed here shall be filtered out (all arguments in 6.3.2.4 set to 0), when security is
enabled, but not yet established.
Empty OAM frames (just the OAM header, without any CADs):
- Shall pass without checks before LKs are installed
- Shall pass security after LKs are installed
All other OAM messages need to pass the security based on its current configuration. If the security
is active, all containers, except those OAM containers listed above, shall be protected.
LinkLayerSec.process_incoming_message shall do the following processing in this order:
•
If the incoming message is any of the above listed OAM messages exempt from security, skip
the remaining processing steps.
•
Determine which Key Slot state applies based on KeySwitch (Header) Flag (0 for first slot, 1
for second). The Key Slot state includes Key, Salt, and“Last Link Layer RX AEAD Invocation”
Counter as well as possible status counters.
•
Check if selected Key Slot is valid and ready. If not, drop messages and increment statistics
counter “security: dropped RX frames” by 1.
•
Construct assumed IV (see section 6.3.1.2 for IV format and section 6.3.1.3 for container
format):
o Split “Last Link Layer RX AEAD Invocation Counter” in two parts:
▪ Last Shadow Counter: | the most significant 56 bits
▪ Last Counter: | the least significant 8 bits
o If Last Counter < received Counter (see 6.3.1.3.1):
▪ Assume “AEAD Invocation Counter” for incoming containerprocessing as:
•
Last Shadow Counter as the most significant 56 bits
•
Received Counter as the least significant 8 bits
o If Last Counter >= received Counter (see 6.3.1.3.1):
▪ Assume “AEAD Invocation Counter” for incoming containerprocessing as:
•
Last Shadow Counter + 1 as the most significant 56 bits
•
Received Counter as the least significant 8 bits
•
Do crypto processing (by running AES-GMAC or AES-GCM based on configuration)
•
Check ICV:
o If this fails, drop messages, call the primitive defined in section 6.3.2.5.
o If ICV correct:
▪ Update “Last Link Layer RX AEAD Invocation Counter” with value of assumed
“AEAD Invocation Counter”.
▪ AES-GMAC: Return container without counter and ICV (see 6.3.2.4).
▪ AES-GCM: Return container with decrypted payload and remove counter and
ICV (see 6.3.2.4).
▪ Switch the active RX Key Slot, if message was received with correct ICV of the
other Key Slot. Deactivate old Key Slot.

The following incoming OAM messages shall pass without checks and modifications by the link layer

All OAM frames/messages with KeyEx primitives
•

o Node Discover
o Self Announce
OAM messages not listed here shall be filtered (all arguments in 6.3.2.2 set to 0), when security is

- Shall pass security after LKs are installed
All other OAM messages need to pass the security based on its current configuration. If the security
is active, all containers, except those OAM containers listed above, shall be protected.
LinkLayerSec.process_outgoing_message shall do the following processing in this order:
•
If the incoming message is any of the above listed OAM messages exempt from security, skip
the remaining processing steps.
•
In the Security Payload, set byte0, bit7=1
•
Select the Key, Salt, Next Link Layer TX AEAD Invocation Counter, and Status based on
currently selected key slot.
•
Check if selected Key Slot is "ready" or "active". If not, drop messages and increment
statistics counter “security: dropped TX frames” (see3.4.3) by 1. Call primitive 6.3.2.5.
•
Construct IV (see section 6.3.1.2 for IV format and section 6.3.1.3 for container format):
o Construct IV by concatenating the fields:
▪ KeyEx = 0
▪ Dir

heading: 6.4 Key Exchange
text:
▪ Salt
▪ “Next Link Layer TX AEAD Invocation Counter”
o Increment “Next Link LayerTX AEAD Invocation Counter” by 1
o Check IV “Link Layer TX AEAD Invocation Counter” regarding margin to overflow (the
remaining value range of the counter before overflow):
▪ If the margin to overflow drops below 10%, call primitive
KeyEx.report_status_LK (0x81).
▪ If the margin to overflow drops below 5%, call primitive
KeyEx.report_status_LK (0x81).
▪ Upon reaching its maximum value, the current Key Slot shall be deactivated,
and the other key slot shall be selected. Then, the primitive
KeyEx.report_status_LK (0x81) shall be called.
•
Process Container Header, Counter and DLL Payload with AES-GCM or AES-GMAC based on
configuration
•
Construct Security Payload
o Add least significant 8 bits of the constructed IV as counter.
o Add processed DLL payload.
o Add ICV.
•
Call primitive 6.3.2.2.

section_title: Mapping Primitives to OAM messages (Link Layer Security)
heading: 6.3.5 Mapping Primitives to OAM messages (Link Layer Security)
text:
6.3.5 Mapping Primitives to OAM messages (Link Layer Security)
All primitives of the Link Layer Security shall not be accessible through the OAM channel or external
interfaces since this would break security.
Key Exchange

section_title: General Concepts for Key Exchange (KeyEx) Primitives
heading: 6.4.1 General Concepts for Key Exchange (KeyEx) Primitives
text:
6.4.1 General Concepts for Key Exchange (KeyEx) Primitives
The concepts in the following subsections are shared between many primitives.

heading: 6.4.1.1 Locations of Key Exchange Entities
text:
6.4.1.1 Locations of Key Exchange Entities
For an ASA Root Device, the Key Exchange Entity shall be located at the ASA Root ECU Software.
For an ASA Root Device, there shall be one Key Exchange Entity per ASA Branch.
For a non-Root ASA Device, the Key Exchange Entity shall be located at the ASA Device itself.

heading: 6.4.1.2 Definitions
text:
6.4.1.2 Definitions
The following terms are used for describing the primitives:
•
Implicit Data: parameters that are authenticated but not transmitted and not encrypted.
They are usually determined by other header fields (e.g. header fields in the OAM).
•
Additional Data: parameters that are authenticated and transmitted but not encrypted.
•
Data (encrypted): parameters that are authenticated, encrypted, and transmitted.
•
Enc.: Encrypted (yes, no, n/a)–n/a meaning “not applicable”.
•
Auth.: Authenticated (yes, no, n/a)–n/a meaning “not applicable”.

section_title: Status and Error Codes for KeyEx primitives
heading: 6.4.1.3 Status and Error Codes for KeyEx primitives
text:
6.4.1.3 Status and Error Codes for KeyEx primitives
The 8bit status codes shall be defined as follows:
•
0x00: OK.
•
0x10: Nonce Computation not finished yet.
•
0x11: Authentication failed.
•
0x12: Wrong UUID.
•
0x20: Already written before and can only be written once.
•
0x21: Written but verify failed.
•
0x30: UUID not written to device yet.
•
0x40: Device Key Part 0 not written to device yet.
•
0x41: Device Key Part 1 not written to device yet.
•
0x42: Binding Key not written to device yet.
•
0x43: Maximum number of writes reached.
•
0x44: Link Key not written to device yet.
•
0x50: Not enough LKs.
•
0x51: Too many LKs.
•
0x52: Unsupported LK size.
•
0x53: Unsupported Salt size.
•
0x60: Unsupported Key Slot
•
0x61: Key Slot empty
•
0x62: Key Slot deactivated before
•
0xFF: Unspecified error (optional).
Relevant Status / Error codes per primitive are shown in Appendix A: KeyEx Primitive–Mapping of
Status Codes.

section_title: Initialization Vector Construction for KeyEx primitives
heading: 6.4.1.4 Initialization Vector Construction for KeyEx primitives
text:
6.4.1.4 Initialization Vector Construction for KeyEx primitives
The 96bit IV for the protection of KeyEx primitives shall be constructed as follows:
•
[95:95] KeyEx = 1
•
[94:94] Direction (see section 6.4.1.7)
•
[93:64] Salt–as installed by the KeyEx or 0 if not.
•
[63:32] Power Cycle Counter as defined by the Root Device
•
[31:00] KeyEx AEAD Invocation Counter

section_title: Cryptography and AEAD construction for KeyEx primitives
heading: 6.4.1.5 Cryptography and AEAD construction for KeyEx primitives
text:
6.4.1.5 Cryptography and AEAD construction for KeyEx primitives
The messages shall be protected and encrypted by AES-GCM.
The device shall support AES-GCM with AES128.
The device may additionally support AES-GCM with AES256.

heading: 6.4.1.6 Integrity Check Value Construction
text:
6.4.1.6 Integrity Check Value Construction
Informational: Secured Key Exchange Primitives require the use of an Integrity Check Value (ICV).
The ICV shall be constructed from the fields defined in the respective primitive using Network Byte
Order (Big Endian), where the order of fields is identical to the order in the primitive definition.

heading: 6.4.1.7 Generic Fields for KeyEx
text:
6.4.1.7 Generic Fields for KeyEx
The “ID” shall be auint8 field defined as a unique number per KeyEx primitive.
The “Direction” shall be auint8 field defined as follows:
•
0x00: message from Root to Device.
•
0x01: message from Device to Root.
•
0x02-0xff: reserved (don’t use).
Informational: The “Direction” field will be used for secured KeyEx primitives as implicit data.

section_title: State Values for Link Keys (used in Status_LK)
heading: 6.4.1.8 State Values for Link Keys (used in Status_LK)
text:
6.4.1.8 State Values for Link Keys (used in Status_LK)
The Link Key States used in Status_LK shall be defined as follows:
•
0b00: Empty–No key installed
•
0b01: Ready–Key installed but not active yet
•
0b11: Active–Key installed and in usage
•
0b10: Deactivated–Key installed but deactivated (for RX: received valid switch to different
slot, for TX: other slot got activated by KeyEx OAM message).

section_title: Ordering of repeatable fields (used in Status_LK)
heading: 6.4.1.9 Ordering of repeatable fields (used in Status_LK)
text:
6.4.1.9 Ordering of repeatable fields (used in Status_LK)
Parameters and return values for primitives regarding Link Keys always shall order the repeatable
fields in ascending order of the nodeIDs, to which they belong.
Nodes, which have their security policy set to none, have to be listed with all zero values.

section_title: Mapping of Primitives to OAM messages (KeyEx)
heading: 6.4.2 Mapping of Primitives to OAM messages (KeyEx)
text:
6.4.2 Mapping of Primitives to OAM messages (KeyEx)
All fields in OAM messages shall be in Big Endian (BE).
Reserved Bytes shall be set to 0x00 on sending and ignored on receiving.
TheIDfield refers to the KeyExchange Primitive ID.
TheParametersfield refers to the KeyExchange Primitive Parameters without additional stuffing
bytes.
Each KeyEx OAM Message shall be transported in an exclusive Container and shall not be grouped
with other OAM Messages, therefore CADnext field (see 5.5.3) shall always be 0.
Informational: The Status Code of a KeyExchange Response is included in theParametersfield (Byte
0).

heading: 6.4.2.1 Key Exchange Requests

Informational: Key Exchange Requests use the OAM Command 0x7D which is reserved for Security.
For requests the OAM structure mapping shall be like this (Bytes counted after the OAM Header):
Byte | Bit(s) | Value | Description

6:0 | 0x7C | Command
7:0 | ID | Primitive ID

section_title: Primitives of the Key Exchange Entity (KeyEx)
heading: 6.4.3 Primitives of the Key Exchange Entity (KeyEx)
text:
6.4.3 Primitives of the Key Exchange Entity (KeyEx)
Primitives with an even ID (least significant bit = 0) shall be used for unprotected/unencrypted
operations.
For all KeyEx primitives the AEAD is based on the layout of the OAM message for this primitive.
Primitive parameter fields are mapped to OAM Messages in the order, in which they are given, each
field is mapped with its MSByte first.

6.4.3.6 KeyEx.setup_policy (ID: 0x08)
This primitive is used to set the policy for one or more nodes.
This primitive includes the Node_Policies struct:
•

•
