o Node [uint8]
▪ NodeID [7…3], Bitmask 0b11111000
▪ Reserved [2…0], Bitmask 0b00000111, shall be all 0 on TX and ignored on RX
o Policy [uint8]:
▪ 0: No Security
▪ 1: Authentication only
▪ 3: Authentication and Encryption
▪ 2, 4-255: Reserved
This primitive changes the read-only ASA Security Register defined in Section 3.4.1.
If the PCN does not fit the current PCN of the device, this command is not executed and returns
status 0xFF.
If the PCN matches, the Node Security Policies are set accordingly to the Node_Policies struct.
If the parameter Persist is set to 1, the Node Security Policies included shall be stored persistently
and it shall not be possible to change them again. (This only includes the Nodes present in the
struct).
If one of the included Node Security Policies has been persistently written before, the return code
0x20 shall be used and no policy shall be changed.
If persistently storing the Node Security Policy fails, the return code 0x21 shall be used.
All changes in Node Security Policy take effect at the beginning of the next link startup, regardless
whether it has been written persistently or non-persistently.

heading: 6.4.4 Key Exchange Phases (Informational)
text: 6.4.4 Key Exchange Phases (Informational)

heading: 6.4.4.1 Startup
text:
6.4.4.1 Startup
•
The Root Device shall have knowledge of the sets (UUID, NodeID) of all branch ASA devices.
Missing relations shall be built by fetching the UUIDs of the respective nodes on startup.
•
A Device shall generate thePower Cycle Nonce (PCN)that should be random and different at
every startup. This shall be finished before answering the first KeyEx.read_current_nonce
request. In case the Power Cycle Nonce is not generated on KeyEx.read_current_nonce
request, the Device shall answer with the error code 0x10 (see section 6.4.1.3) The PCN shall
be identical for all KeyEx.read_current_nonce request in a single power cycle.
•
The Root Node has to guarantee that thePower Cycle Counter (PCC)increments on each
Power Cycle.

section_title: UUID and Device Key Tier-1 Installation
heading: 6.4.4.2 UUID and Device Key Tier-1 Installation
text:
6.4.4.2 UUID and Device Key Tier-1 Installation
In the Tier-1 production, a process similar to this and based on the OEM requirements shall be run
for a given device:
•
Generate a UUID and DK_0 using a usable scheme, so that both are unique.
•
Install a UUID using KeyEx.install_UUID
•
Install a DK_0 using KeyEx.install_DK_0_unencrypted
•
Handle the returned status of the calls.

section_title: Device Key OEM and Binding Key Installation (encrypted)
heading: 6.4.4.3 Device Key OEM and Binding Key Installation (encrypted)

figures.title: Simplified Process of DK_1 and BK Installation (function names not binding!)

text:
6.4.4.3 Device Key OEM and Binding Key Installation (encrypted)
The following process shall be run to securely install the DK_1 and BK (e.g. in an untrusted
environment) for 1 or more devices:
•
For each device:
o Read out the UUID using KeyEx.read_UUID
o Read out the Key Status using KeyEx.read_status_keys
•
Based on the information read out, acquire the encrypted payloads for installing via
KeyEx.install_DK_1_encrypted and KeyEx.install_BK_encrypted
•
For each device:
o Install DK_1 using KeyEx.install_DK_1_encrypted
o Install BK using KeyEx.install_BK_encrypted
o Collect returned proofs and status
o Read out the Key Status using KeyEx.read_status_keys
•
Evaluate proofs and key status.
The following figure gives a short overview of this process (function names are descriptive and do
not match the primitive names defined in this document)
Figure 6-3: Simplified Process of DK_1 and BK Installation (function names not binding!)

section_title: Device Key OEM and Binding Key Installation (unencrypted)
heading: 6.4.4.4 Device Key OEM and Binding Key Installation (unencrypted)
text:
6.4.4.4 Device Key OEM and Binding Key Installation (unencrypted)
The following process shall only be run to install the DK_1 and BK in a trusted environment for 1 or
more devices:
•
For each device:
o Read out the UUID using KeyEx.read_UUID
o Read out the Key Status using KeyEx.read_status_keys
•
Based on the information read out, acquire the payloads for installing via
KeyEx.install_DK_1_unencrypted and KeyEx.install_BK_encrypted_by_DK_1_only
•
For each device:
o Install DK_1 using KeyEx.install_DK_1_unencrypted
o Install BK using KeyEx.install_BK_encrypted_by_DK_1_only
o Collect returned proofs
o Read out key status
•
Evaluate proofs and key status.
Warning: This process can only be run in a trusted environment since an attacker could recover the
installed keys! You should use the“Device Key OEM and Binding Key Installation (encrypted)”, if
possible.

heading: 6.4.4.5 Link Key Installation

figures.title: Simplified Process of Link Key Installation (function names not binding!)
Message Flow: Key Rotation on impending IV Overflow (function names not binding!)

text:
6.4.4.5 Link Key Installation
The Root ECU consists of a Software (Root SW) and an ASA chip (Root Device).
The following procedure shall run on every link key installation process (that is when installing link
keys in all devices).
On Startup, both Key Slots (0 and 1) will undergo this process, on LK installation due to IV overflow
(KeyEx.report_status_LK, 0x81 with inactivated key slot) only the affected Key Slot will undergo this
process:
•
The Root Node shall request all PCNs of the devices, LKs need to be installed into.
•
The Root Node may request the UUID of all devices, if not stored.
•
The Root ECU shall generate the LKs and Salts:
o LKs shall be unique per link.
o Salts shall be unique per device and “KeyEx.install_LKs_encrypted”message.
•
The Root Node shall initialize its “KeyEx AEAD Invocation Counter” used for creating the IV of
outgoing KeyEx messages with 1.
•
The Root Node shall initialize its Salt used for creating the IV of outgoing KeyEx messages
with a random number.
•
The Root Node shall construct the IV for all outgoing messages based on the rules in section
6.4.1.4.
•
The Root Node shall install the LKs and Salts into the devices using the
“KeyEx.install_LKs_encrypted”message (see section 6.4.3.12 for details).
•
A Device shall check the incoming “KeyEx.install_LKs_encrypted” messages at least like this:
o Device shall check IV:
▪ KeyEx bit shall be 1, if not drop message and return status “Authentication failed
(0x11)”.
▪ Direction bit shall be 0 (Root to Device), if not drop message and return
“Authentication failed (0x11)”.
▪ Salt shall be the same for all KeyEx message in this power cycle, if not drop
message and return status “Authentication failed (0x11)”.
▪ Power Cycle Counter shall be the same for all KeyEx message in this power cycle,
if not drop message and return status “Authentication failed (0x11)”.
▪ The “KeyEx AEAD Invocation Counter” shall be larger than the previously received
value (receive counter initialized with 0). If this is not the case, drop and return
status “Authentication failed (0x11)”.
o Device shall check that the UUID matches the devices UUID. If not drop message and
return status “Wrong UUID (0x12)”.
o Device shall check the ICV.
o Device shall decrypt LKs and Salts.
o Device shall install LKs and Salts in the respective Key Slot.
o Device shall startup/unblock Link Layer Protection.
o Device shall update IV:
▪ If no KeyEx primitive received in power cycle, store Power Cycle Counter and
update receive IV counter to value.
▪ Set IV to received value.
o Device shall only generate a proof as answer (that is including IV and ICV), if status is 0
(OK):
▪ Generate IV based on section 6.4.1.4.
▪ Generate ICV based on section 6.4.1.6.
•
The Root Nodeshall check the response of the “KeyEx.install_LKs_encrypted” at least like
this:
o Root Node shall check IV, if present:
▪ Check that IV is increasing.
o Root Node shall check ICV, if present.
▪ Check the ICV using KeyEx bit = 1, Direction = 1 (upstream).
▪ Check the ICV based on installed Salt and Key.
o Root Node shall use status.
The following figure gives an overview if the Link Key installation for a link made up by Device B and
Device C.

heading: 7.3 Common ASEP Format Basics

tables.title: ASEP stream types

figures.title: Common ASEP packet format

text:
ASA Application Stream Encapsulation Protocol (ASEP)
ASA Application Stream Encapsulation Protocol (ASEP) defines the format, in which application data
is provided to the transmitting data link layer over the DLP_TX.
There is a multitude of stream types in the ASA Application Stream Encapsulation Protocol (ASEP).
Each defines one or more ASEP packet types including header and value field(s).
The Application Stream Encapsulator (ASE) acts as a transmitter on a DLP_TX whereas the Application
Stream Decapsulator (ASD) acts as a receiver on a DLP_RX. Each ASE and ASD on a specific Data Link
Layer Port supports only a single ASEP (see 3.5.1.2).
INFORMATIVE: A possible communication between an ASE and ASD in the same node for the
construction of an ASEP transceiver for bidirectional protocols is up to the implementer.
Application Stream Encapsulator
The ASE converts application stream data units into an ASEP format, where it has to handle header,
payload and footer generation as well as fragmentation into Data Link Layer Containers.
The ASE communicates with the Data Link Layer via the primitives defined in 5.6.1.
For a specific timeout dependent on the stream type andapplication, the ASE shall indicate a “data
starve event”, when expected application data units are not being received, in the register 3.6.2.
Application Stream Decapsulator
The ASD converts an ASEP format into application data units. It has to execute the reassembly of
fragmented ASEP frames as well as handle errors. Reassembly errors resulting in verifiably corrupt
application data units have to be recorded in 3.7.1.
The ASD communicates with the Data Link Layer via the primitives defined in 5.7.1.

text:
7.3.3 Common ASEP Format Basics per Footer
An ASEP format may or may not employ a CRC checksum over one ASEP packet, which gets sent and
may get fragmented into several Data Link Layer Containers. A CRC checksum might also be
separately generated for ASEP header and ASEP payload.
If the ASEP format does employ a CRC check, the ASD shall check the consistency of the data after
reassembly of the received fragments and shall indicate an error by incrementing 3.7.1.

heading: 7.5.4 Usage of Format
text:
7.5.4 Usage of Format
This subsection 7.5.4 is INFORMATIVE.
Byte mode is emulating bidirectional I2C mode on a byte-per-byte/bit basis. I2C condition bits are
transmitted.
Bulk mode is accumulating I2C commands of the same kind. I2C condition bits are implied.
I2C is bidirectional and accordingly, both ASE and ASD have one DLP_TX connection and DLP_RX
connection.
I2C Slave address 000_1000 is recommended to be assigned to the root node I2C Slave (connected to
ASE) for communication with that ASA node.
I2C Slave address 000_1001 is recommended to be assigned to the non-root I2C multi-mode
Master/Slave (connected to ASD) for communication with that ASA node.

heading: 7.6.2 Usage of Format
text:
7.6.2 Usage of Format
This entire subsection is informative.
An Ethernet Gateway connecting to an ASA device may require several logical point-2-point tunnels
to be configured inside the ASA SerDes Branch.

heading: 7.7 ASEP Format: SPI
text:
Buffers are required to adapt input Ethernet line rate to ASA allocated bandwidth. Buffers are also
required to adapt ASA allocated bandwidth to output Ethernet line rate.
ASEP Format: SPI
This ASEP is based on segmenting SPI bus activity into fixed size chunksof length “SPI data
conversion period”, where each chunk is transmitted in one ASEP packet. The response to the SPI
master has a defined latency and SPI access has to be handled in a special way. See 7.7.1 for cycle
time definitions and 7.7.2 for requirements on SPI interface.
Informative: The SPI interface pin names are Serial Clock SCK, Master In Slave Out MISO, Master In
Slave Out MOSI and Chip Select CS.

section_title: SPI Cycle Time Definitions and ASE Behavior
heading: 7.7.1 SPI Cycle Time Definitions and ASE Behavior
text: 7.7.1 SPI Cycle Time Definitions and ASE Behavior

heading: 7.7.1.1 SPI DLL Schedule Transmission Cycle
text:
7.7.1.1 SPI DLL Schedule Transmission Cycle
The“SPIDLL schedule transmission cycle”(SPI_STC) is defined as the maximum duration (within a
programmed DLL schedule) from the start of a first SPI ASE DLL schedule slot to the start of a second
SPI ASE DLL schedule slot, while during this period the SPI ASD has received an ASEP packet once at
least. The SPI_STC is measured as integer multiple of TDD cycles.

heading: 7.7.1.2 SPI ASEP Data Conversion Period
text:
7.7.1.2 SPI ASEP Data Conversion Period
The“SPI ASEPdata conversion period” (SPI_DCP) is defined as the duration of SPI bus activity (on
master side) converted into one SPI ASEP packet.
SPI_DCP has to be equal or larger than SPI_STC.

heading: 7.7.1.3 SPI Turnaround Time
text:
7.7.1.3 SPI Turnaround Time
The SPI turnaround time (SPI_TAT) is defined as an integer multiple of SPI_DCP. It denotes the time
on the SPI interface between a data conversion block from the SPI master to the response data block
out of the SPI-over-ASA tunnel to the SPI master.
The start point for counting the turnaround time is when the buffering of the first SPI data block of
the SPI frame into the ASA device (ASE memory) is complete. The turnaround time stops, when the
first SPI bit (in response) is on the SPI interface.
The ASE/ASD of the ASA device connected to the SPI master controls the data buffering time in order
to keep the turnaround time of SPI return data constant. The ASE/ASD counts the turnaround time
by using the PTB clock frequency/4 (nominally 16nsec resolution).
Informative: The ASA-internal mandatory PTB is used as time base, but the events on the external
(outside ASA compliant portion) SPI interface start and stop the timer.

heading: 7.7.1.4 ASE Behavior in Root Node
text:
7.7.1.4 ASE Behavior in Root Node
On the start of an SPI frame, the ASE waits SPI_DCP to record data to construct an SPI ASEP data
mode packet.
If the same SPI frame continues for more than one SPI_DCP, starting from the second SPI ASEP data
mode packet, all the SPI data buffered shall be sent immediately via the DLP_TX.dataUnit when a
DLP_TX.indicateSlot is received (see 5.6.1).
Informative: For longer SPI frames, this will eventually lead to no waiting times for (the last bit of) SPI
data for any valid combination of SPI_STC and SPI_DCP and ensures a guaranteed SPI_TAT as short as
possible in the schedule and ASA branch.

heading: 7.7.1.5 ASE Behavior in Non-Root Node
text:
7.7.1.5 ASE Behavior in Non-Root Node
The ASE shall always respond with an SPI ASEP data mode packet of the same length as the
corresponding one received from the ASE in the root node.

heading: 7.7.1.6 ASEP impact on timing
text:
7.7.1.6 ASEP impact on timing
The SPI ASEP does not fully maintain SPI bus timing, especially for SPI idle gaps. The minimum SPI idle
gap shall be used to enable compatibility with connected SPI devices. This SPI idle gaps has to be
taken into consideration for payload reservation.
For multiple SPI frames inside one DCP, the last frames position within the DCP is captured and can
be reconstructed.
If precise timing is required for the SPI bus interface, the common ASEP mechanism with PTB
presentation times has to be used and payload data rate adjusted accordingly.

section_title: Additional Requirements to Tunneled SPI Interface on an ASA device
heading: 7.7.2 Additional Requirements to Tunneled SPI Interface on an ASA device
text: 7.7.2 Additional Requirements to Tunneled SPI Interface on an ASA device

section_title: SPI Master Function and ASA Device Interfacing to SPI Master
heading: 7.7.2.1 SPI Master Function and ASA Device Interfacing to SPI Master
text:
7.7.2.1 SPI Master Function and ASA Device Interfacing to SPI Master
The SPI master shall order read/write accesses in such a way, that within and given window of length
SPI_DCP, there is at maximum one write access and at maximum one read access.
The SPI master side clock rate SCK satisfies the condition: M_SCK*SPI_STC < 160 bytes, i.e. the
Master side SPI influx data rate is kept below average reserved data rate in ASA schedule.
The ASA device interfacing to the SPI master shall offer a mechanism to allow for the ASA device
receiving SPI read/write commands and with latency returning read data.
Informative: For instance, by using 2 distinct SPI CS signals, the SPI master may distinguish the
transmit data to the SPI ASE of an ASA device and the read data from the SPI ASD of the same device.
These two SPI CS signals are allowed to be active at the same time, i.e. write-only, read-only and
simultaneous read-write are possible.

section_title: SPI Slave Function and ASA Device Interfacing to SPI Slave
heading: 7.7.2.2 SPI Slave Function and ASA Device Interfacing to SPI Slave
text:
7.7.2.2 SPI Slave Function and ASA Device Interfacing to SPI Slave
The SPI master on the ASD of ASA device (branch or leaf) connected to the SPI slave is able to stop
issuing the SCK to pause the SPI communication when the ASD receives an empty SPI packet from
ASA node interfacing to the SPI master (root).
The SPI slave side clock rate SCK satisfies the condition: S_SCK*SPI_STC ≥ 128bytes, i.e. the
maximum payload sent in one container can locally be turned around on the SPI within SPI_STC. The
MOSI buffer at the SPI slave side is never fuller than 128 bytes and the latency of the turnaround to
gather the response data is SPI_STC at maximum.

heading: 7.9.2 Overview

figures.title: Encapsulated channels of DP (informative)

text:
7.9.2 Overview
The eDP ASEP provides encapsulation formats for the unidirectional Main Link and bi-directional AUX
channel. The Main Link data is encapsulated in the same order as produced by the DP link layer;
either in Essential Data Mode (EDM) or Plain Lane Mode (PLM). The AUX channel is transmitted
bidirectional always completing a transaction. VESA DP defined mechanisms of the Stream/Link
Policy Maker (see [asep_dp_01], section 2.1) are untouched by this specification.

heading: 7.9.2.1 Encapsulated Features
text:
7.9.2.1 Encapsulated Features
In Essential Data Mode, this ASEP supports encapsulation of:
- SST Stream Source with a symbol size of 8bit (8b/10b mapping), including
o MSA
o SDP
o VB-ID
o Mvid
o Maud
o Dummy bytes
- DSC-compressed Stream Source
- HDCP-encrypted Stream Source
In Plain Lane Mode, the complete lane-allocated PHY Layer coded stream is encapsulated.
Informative: This is a fail-safe mode with full DP compatibility.
The AUX_CH is separate from the Main Link and always encapsulated the same way.
Informative: As the eDP ASEP encapsulates the basic data fields or Transfer Units of the DP standard,
future updates with backward compatibility within DP like the Automotive Extensions are inherently
supported.

7.9.2.3 Relation of ASEP Coding to DP Coding
The eDP ASEP packets for the Main Link packs in Data Symbols, Komma Symbols and Stuffed Data
Symbols without the coding overhead of the VESA DP physical layer.

Figure 7-6: Composition of a frame in DP (informative)
The eDP ASEP builds on the VESA defined lane byte order mapping (including zero padding), see
[asep_dp_01] section 2.2.1.3. Komma characters are only transmitted once per occurrence
(regardless of the number of lanes coded), but VB-ID, Mvid and Maud are transmitted duplicated 4
times to fulfill VESA specification (see [asep_dp_01] Figure 2-12).
In the case of DSC, Compressed Data is being transmitted instead of Data Symbols (see [asep_dp_01]
section 2.8.4.4).
In the case of HDCP, "... in SST mode, all data symbols (including video data, secondary data and
dummy symbols) must be encrypted and K-codes must not be encrypted." (see [asep_dp_03],
section 3.1).
This means, the Komma Symbols are present as delimiters of data in all supported scenarios and are
therefore used as start and end markers of eDP ASEP packets.
When no HDCP is used, Stuffed Data Symbols between FS and FE can be decided to be dropped (not
encapsulated). Valid data of consecutive Transfer Units is then transmitted combined in one Main
Link ASEP packet, i.e. one video line.
The mandatory presence of the DP FEC for DSC compressed streams is to provide an error-correcting
capability for a data format, where individual bit errors can affect entire slices instead of single pixels.
The ASA physical layer FEC provides at least the same integrity protection and applies to all data.
HDCP on top of a DSC compressed stream is also an option. Since the HDCP cipher does not advance
in cycles carrying DP FEC control codes, the integrity of the encrypted data stream is given, see
[asep_dp_01] section 3.5.1.5.1.
The eDP ASEP packet for the AUX encapsulates one transaction per packet.

heading: 7.9.2.4 Plain Lane Encapsulation Modes
text:
7.9.2.4 Plain Lane Encapsulation Modes
Plain lane encapsulation modes are defined for the DP 8b/10b Link Layer and for the DP 128b/132b
Link Layer. In these modes, the fully coded out of the Main-Link PHY Logical Sublayer is encapsulated
(see Figure 2-8 in [asep_dp_01], where the reference point is output of “Encoder”; or Figure 3-29 in
[asep_dp_01], where the reference point is output of “Pre-Coding”;).

ASEP Format: I2S
7.10.1Features
The I2S ASEP supports data formats for all common bit widths in mono, stereo and multi-channel
(time-division multiplex, TDM).
The I2S ASEP supports I2S timing master to be at either I2S TX or I2S RX.
The I2S ASEP codes audio frequency explicitly for most common values and supports a derivation off
of PTB time stamps.
7.10.1.1Audio Sampling Rate to PTB Synchronization
For this method, the ASE connecting to the I2S device in master mode shall capture PTB time stamps
every “N” cycles of the SCK(serial clock of the I2S) or MCK (audio master clock) signal and shall
transmit them. SCK and MCK a related by an integer factor defined in 3.5.8.3.
The non-master mode side can reconstruct the audio sampling rate as a ratio of PTB clock and N:

The sections 8.2 through 8.5 (MLE) mirror the sections 4.2 through 4.5 (ML).
If there is no change given in the respective subsection 8.{section subnumbering}, the corresponding
subsection 4.{section subnumbering} is referenced directly after the section headlinewith “See
equivalent subsection in section 4”and applies to the MLE Physical Layer without any alterations,
except with section references changes from 4.x.y.z to 8.x.y.z (where x.y.z represent the section
subnumbering of any hierarchy depth).
If this equivalancy is given for a section 8.x, the entire section 4.x is valid including its entire sub-
hierachy of chapters 4.x.y.z (where y.z represent the section subnumbering of any hierarchy depth).
If any changes are required, the subsections are replaced as a whole. A new subsection with same
subnumbering is created in section 8. For these altered sections, the entire corresponding subsection
in section 4 does not apply.

TDD (8.2.2.2) with one difference: the input data to the physical layer is equal to all zeros except for
the last physical layer block in each burst (see below).
The first bit being sent of the resynchronization header is its LSB. The first bit being sent of the
physical layer block (except the last one) is its MSB. The first bit being sent of the last physical layer
block is its LSB.
The number of symbols in the quiet gap is the same as in normal mode (see Table 8-3).
The last physical layer block is identical to PhaseSGA as defined in Equation 8-1.
The PCS Scrambler is being run as described in 8.2.2.5.1 for all MLE modes.
For MLE modes derived of Speed Grades 4 and 5, scrambled physical layer block symbols and
symbols of Equation 8-1 are mapped to PAM4 as in normal mode (4.2.2.7), scrambled symbols of all
MLE modes derived of Speed Grades 1,2 and 3 are mapped to PAM2 as in normal mode (4.2.2.6).

See section 8.6.2.3 for the 4b/b5 encoding and control characters. Each physical layer block takes
10 bits of encoded fragmented OAM data, or two 4b/5b characters.
Before the first byte of the OAM frame, one group of two control characters JJ and then (in the next
physical layer block) one group of two control characters JK are transmitted to mark SOP (start of
packet).
Each byte of OAM frame data is 4b/5b encoded.
Each byte of the section 5.5 OAM frame is fed (in ascending byte order) into the CRC8 checksum
calculator (see section 8.6.2.4). The resulting 8 bits of the checksum are also 4b/5b encoded.
There CRC8 resets for every OAM frame.
After the last byte of the OAM frame, one group of TI is transmitted to mark EOP (end of packet).
Outside of SOP, OAM frame data and EOP, a group of II is transmitted per physical layer block to
mark IDLE.

heading: 8.6.2.2 PTB time stamping
text:
8.6.2.2 PTB time stamping
The PTB time stamp in the header of the OAM frame is taken, when the group of two control
characters JK of the SOP passes the transmitting MDI.

heading: 8.6.2.3 4b/5b Encoder

tables.title: 4b/5b Encoding
4b/5b Control Characters

text:
8.6.2.3 4b/5b Encoder
The 4b/b5 encoding process maps 4 bits of data to a 5 bit code word as depicted in the following
table:
4b/5b code | 4b/5b code
Data[3:0] | Data[3:0]
word [4:0] | word [4:0]
Table 8-14: 4b/5b Encoding
The 4b/5b code also contains the following control symbols:
Symbol | 4b/5b code | Description
word [4:0]
H | Halt
I | Idle
J | Start #1
K | Start #2
L | Start #3
Q | Quiet
R | Reset
S | Set
T | Terminate (End)
Table 8-15: 4b/5b Control Characters

heading: 8.6.2.4 CRC8 Definition
text:
8.6.2.4 CRC8 Definition
The cyclic redundancy check shall use the polynomial 0xA6.
The starting value of the CRC is 0xFF.
The appendix (XOR value) of the CRC is 0xFF.
The input data shall be used byte-wise reflected.
The result data shall be used reflected.

heading: 8.6.3 Secondary Control Channel
text:
8.6.3 Secondary Control Channel
The secondary control channel is optional. Its presence is being indicated by the first bit of the
physical layer block, see Table 8-5.

heading: 8.8 Link Aggregation Sublayer
text: Receive Interface Adaptation Layer

heading: 8.7.1.1 Rate Matching
text:
8.7.1.1 Rate Matching
The receiver shall delete all control blocks of Block Type 0x1ewith all control codes set to “Skip
||R||” 0x1C.

heading: 8.7.2.1 Synchronization to SOP and EOP
text:
8.7.2.1 Synchronization to SOP and EOP
The receiver shall scan for SOP character to detect the start of a frame.
The receiver marks the time the when the group of two control characters JK of the SOP passed the
receiving MDI. If the OAM message will be used to initialize the PTB, the delta between the received
time and the time the message was processed will be added to the timestamp prior to initializing the
PTB.

heading: 8.7.2.2 Reassembly & Integrity Check
text:
8.7.2.2 Reassembly & Integrity Check
The 4b/5b decoded OAM frame bytes shall be checked versus the received integrity checksum and
mismatching OAM frames shall be discarded. The number of OAM frames failing integrity checksum
will be counted in 3.3.24.
Link Aggregation Sublayer
Does not apply to MLE.

IV Appendix D: SPI Tunneling Waveform Examples (Informative)
1. SPI master asserts CS#1 to indicate the SPI
data block needed to be transmitted to ASA
node 2.
2. SPI master issues the SCK.
3. SPI master starts to count the wait time
“5D” time to read the SPI return data.
4. SPI master outputs O_DB#1 (N byte) as
MOSI. At the same time, ASD of ASA node 1
returns MISO, but SPI master discards this
one because SPI master knows the
turnaround time in prior. SPI master
continuesto discard MISO until ‘5D’ time
have passed.
5. ASE temporary stores O_DB#1 and Coded
CS#1 in own buffer memory. The role of
Coded CS is the indication on frame status
(start/end/continuation) of the transmitted
SPI data.
6. After SPI master output all of SPI data of
this SPI frame, SPI master stops issuing SCK
and de assert CS#1.
7. After “D” time has passed, ASEoutput
O_DB#1 with Code CS#1 to the first DLL
assigned to transmit the SPI packet.
8. At the same time, ASE/ASD starts to count
“4D” time by SCK. This “4D” is the fixed
turnaround time.
9. PHY/DLL of ASA node 2 receives and
decodes the up-link packet. ASD decodes
the SPI packet.
10. ASD of ASA node 2 as SPI master on far side
asserts S_CS to start SPI communication
with SPI slave.
11. ASD issues the SCK.
12. ASD outputs O_DB#1 as MOSI.
13. At the same time, SPI slave returns I_DB#1
as MISO.
14. ASD de asserts S_CS to finish the SPI
communication with SPI Slave, according to
the Coded CS information transmitted.
15. ASE of ASA node 2 encodes the I_DB#1 into
SPI data packet and ASE outputs the SPI
data packet to the coming container
assigned to convey SPI data packet.
16. PHY/DLL of ASA node 1 receives and
decodes the down link packet. ASD decodes
the SPI packet.
17. ASD temporary stores I_ODB#1 in own
buffer memory.
18. SPI master has also been continuing time
up to “5D”. After “5D” time (turnaround
time) has passed since the first SPI data
issued, SPI master starts to get the I_DB#1.
Therefore, SPI master assert CS#0 and issue
SCK to read the return SPI data.
19. After “4D” time has passed since the first
SPI data buffered into ASE memory, I_DB#1
has been started to read out from ASD
buffer by SPI master
20. When SPI master completes to get all of the
SPI return data (I_DB#1), the SPI master de
asserted CS#0 to finish the SPI
communication with ASA node 1.

turnaround time “4D” elapses and SPI master
accesses it.
38.When SPI master completes to get all of the SPI
return data (I_DB#2), the SPI master de asserted
CS#0 to finish the SPI communication with ASA
node 1.
Figure IV-2: SPI ASEP tunneling–Single/Multi Write/Read example 2
These procedures are almost same as one in Figure
IV-2.
(1)--(34)
The SPI master does not need the SPI return data
from the SPI slave, then the SPI master does not need
to assert the CS#0 to get the reading data.
The buffer memory of ASD of ASA node 1 has stored
the return SPI data (20), (34).
35.After more than “6D” of time, SPI master can
issue the data destruction command (36) to ASD
by using SPI protocol for ASD of the ASA node 1, if
it’s necessary.
Figure IV-3: SPI ASEP tunneling–Single/Multi Write only example 3
1. SPI master asserts CS#1 to indicate the SPI data
block needed to be transmitted to ASA node 2.
2. SPI master issues the SCK.
3. SPI master starts to count the wait time “5D” time to
read the SPI return data.
4. SPI master outputs O_DB#1 (N byte) as MOSI. At the
same time, ASD of ASA node 1 returns MISO, but SPI
master discards this one because SPI master knows
the turnaround time in prior. SPI master continues
to discard MISO until ‘5D’ time have passed.
5. ASE temporary stores O_DB#1 and Coded CS#1 in
own buffer memory. The role of Coded CS is the
indication on frame status (start/end/continuation)
of the transmitted SPI data.
6. After “D” time has passed, ASE output O_DB#1 with
Code CS#1 to the first DLL assigned to transmit the
SPI packet.
7. At the same time, ASE/ASD starts to count “4D” time
by SCK. This “4D” is the fixed turnaround time.
8. This SPI frame length is longer than “D”. Therefore,
this SPI data is split to be transmitted by ASE
container.
9. In this case, Coded CS is continuation.
10.PHY/DLL of ASA node 2 receives and decodes the up-
link packet. ASD decodes the SPI packet.
11.ASD of ASA node 2 as SPI master on far side asserts
S_CS to start SPI communication with SPI slave.
12.ASD issues the SCK.
13.ASD outputs O_DB#1 as MOSI.
14.At the same time, SPI slave returns I_DB#1 as MISO.
15.ASE of ASA node 2 encodes the I_DB#1 into SPI data
packet and ASE outputs the SPI data packet to the
coming container assigned to convey SPI data
packet.
16.PHY/DLL of ASA node 1 receives and decodes the
down link packet. ASD decodes the SPI packet.
17.ASD temporary stores I_ODB#1 in own buffer
memory.
18.SPI master has also been continuing time up to “5D”.
After“5D” time (turnaround time) has passed since
the first SPI data issued, SPI master starts to get the
I_DB#1. Therefore, SPI master assert CS#0 and issue
SCK to read the return SPI data.After “4D” time has
passed since the first SPI data buffered into ASE
memory, I_DB#1 has been started to read out from
ASD buffer by SPI master.
19.SPI master simultaneously issues the O_ODB#6, but
this DB is just dummy and is NOT transmitted to ASA
node 2, because CS#1 has already been de asserted.
20.There are no transferable SPI data in this uplink
container because O_DB # 3 is still filling the buffer
memory. This SPI packet which indicates that this
packet is empty by using the void flag is transmitted.
21.PHY/DLL of ASA node 2 receives and decodes the up-
link packet. During ASD is outputting O_DB#2 to SPI
slave, ASD decodes the SPI packet and detects this
SPI packet is empty. Therefore, ASD stops issuing
SCK when ASD completes outputting O_DB#2 and
keep pausing SPI communication until getting the
next SPI data packet.
22.PHY/DLL of ASA node 2 receives and decodes the up-
link packet. ASD decodes the SPI packet and detects
this SPI packet is available.
23.ASD issue SCK again to resume the SPI
communication.
24.ASD outputs O_DB#3 as MOSI.
25.SPI master outputs the O_DB#4 as the last SPI data
block.
26.ASE temporary stores O_DB#4 and Coded CS#1 in
own buffer memory. The role of Coded CS is the
indication on frame status (frame end) of the
transmitted SPI data.
27.SPI master de asserts the CS#1 after all of the SPI
data has been output.
28.ASD outputs O_DB#4 as MOSI.
29.At the same time, SPI slave returns I_DB#4 as MISO.
30.ASD stops issuing SCK after all of the O_DB#4 has
been output, because ASD has gotten the status
information of CS#1 by decoding O_DB#4 packet.
31.Then, ASD de asserts S_CS.
32.After SPI master complete to receive all of SPI return
data, SPI master de asserts CS#0 to finish the SPI
communication.

text:
VIIAppendix G: Recommended Mapping of ASA Register Addresses to local I2C
(informative)
Use 7bit addressing with 1111_011 to address the ASA register map(s) on the ASA device (as 10bit
addressing is not supported). Use R/W-bit of first byte in I2C.
Payload starts from second byte. Send a command and the hierarchical ASA register address
preceded by a node/port identifier as payload. The following table shows the complete sequence of
bytes for a write command on the ASA register map.
For a read command, bytes 6 and 7 are not sent. Instead, bytes 6 and 7 are returned by the ASA
device.
Byte Bit(s) Name | Description
7:1 ASA register access | Local I2C address for ASA register map
access
R/W bit | I2C protocol bit
ASA register map command 0: Write
1: Read
6:5 | reserved, set to 0
4:1 node/port identifier | Local identifier for multi-port device (not
identical with ASA nodeID)
ASA register domain[3] | “d” inTable 3-1
7:5 ASA register domain[2:0]
4:0 ASA register subdomain[5:1] “i” inTable 3-1; set to 0 if not ASA register
domain 4 or 5
ASA register subdomain[0]
6:0 ASA register address[14:8] “a” inTable 3-1
7:0 ASA register address[7:0]
7:0 Register data [15:8] | Data to be written (only present on write)
7:0 Register data [7:0]
